papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 目的:脑[18F]-FDG-PET常显示长新冠患者出现神经认知问题时存在脑代谢减低,但其预后价值尚不明确。我们评估了该人群中的[18F]-FDG PET的长期应用价值。材料和方法:我们回顾了前瞻性SYNPOCov 队列研究(NCT05610436)研究,包括WHO定义的长新冠患者,其具有确认的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2感染,并接受了脑PET扫描且随访时间≥1年。最终临床结果由专家裁定委员会判定为良好(无残留残疾)、部分改善(改善但持续残疾)或稳定。PET扫描与年龄和性别匹配的疫情前健康对照组(n=39)进行比较。从显著的脑区簇(体素水平p值<0.05)中提取区域代谢值。结果:共纳入70名患者(48.3±11.9岁;69%女性;随访时间26.4±9.5个月),其中19名、34名和17名分别被归类为良好、部分改善和稳定的临床结果。基线影像学显示四个脑区存在代谢减低:右侧额叶、顶叶和颞叶皮层以及小脑。在之前住院的患者和感染Omicron变异株前的变异株患者中,右侧额叶和颞叶簇的代谢值显著降低(p=≤0.04和p=≤0.03)。然而,基线区域代谢情况及其随访PET扫描(n=30)的纵向变化均与长期临床结果无显著关联。结论:脑[18F]-FDG PET仍然是评估长新冠神经认知障碍中脑部受累的重要生物标志物,揭示与急性疾病严重程度和病毒变异株相关的代谢特征。尽管其不能预测长期预后,但PET结果有助于加深对持续性脑功能障碍潜在因素的理解。试验注册号及注册日期:NCT05610436;2022-01-07

papers.title: Oral health behaviors, perceptions, and educational needs among enlisted South Korean Army soldiers during the COVID-19 pandemic: A cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Preventive oral health care and education are essential for soldiers' health and military readiness. This study investigated oral health behaviors, dental service utilization, oral health perceptions, and educational needs among enlisted South Korean Army soldiers during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 313 enlisted soldiers who visited military dental clinics in Gyeonggi-do, Republic of Korea, from March 24 to April 16, 2021. Descriptive statistics and Pearson's χ2 tests were performed. Overall, 60.4% of participants did not use oral care products, mainly because they did not perceive a need for them (62.9%). Furthermore, 71.9% had not undergone routine dental examinations, 63.6% had not received dental treatment after enlistment, and 91.4% had no oral health education experience during military service. Video-based education was the preferred method (40.6%), and halitosis prevention and management was the most preferred topic (20.4%). Preferred educational methods did not differ significantly according to age, military rank, educational level, or smoking status (all P > .05). Military rank was significantly associated with perceived adequacy of oral care time (P < .001) and the place of dental treatment (P = .048). Routine dental examinations, dental treatment experience, and oral health education experience showed no significant differences according to participants' general characteristics. Preventive oral health services and education were insufficient among enlisted South Korean Army soldiers. Tailored programs reflecting soldiers' needs and preferred learning methods should be developed and evaluated.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study examined oral health behaviors, dental service utilization, perceptions, and educational needs among South Korean Army soldiers during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study included 313 soldiers who visited military dental clinics between March 24 and April 16, 2021. Descriptive statistics and Pearson's χ2 tests were used to analyze the data. Results showed that 60.4% of participants did not use oral care products, primarily due to a lack of perceived need. Routine dental examinations, treatment, and education were also insufficient, with 71.9%, 63.6%, and 91.4% of participants not having undergone these services, respectively. Video-based education was the preferred method, and halitosis prevention was the most desired topic. Educational methods did not vary significantly by age, rank, education level, or smoking status, but rank was linked to perceived oral care adequacy and dental treatment location. The study highlights the need for tailored oral health education programs for soldiers.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 该研究旨在评估 2019 年冠状病毒病大流行期间韩国陆军士兵的口腔健康行为、牙科服务利用率、口腔健康认知和教育需求。

papers.title_zh: Oral health behaviors, perceptions, and educational needs among enlisted South Korean Army soldiers during the COVID-19 pandemic: A cross-sectional study.
papers.source_body_en: Preventive oral health care and education are essential for soldiers' health and military readiness. This study investigated oral health behaviors, dental service utilization, oral health perceptions, and educational needs among enlisted South Korean Army soldiers during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 313 enlisted soldiers who visited military dental clinics in Gyeonggi-do, Republic of Korea, from March 24 to April 16, 2021. Descriptive statistics and Pearson's χ2 tests were performed. Overall, 60.4% of participants did not use oral care products, mainly because they did not perceive a need for them (62.9%). Furthermore, 71.9% had not undergone routine dental examinations, 63.6% had not received dental treatment after enlistment, and 91.4% had no oral health education experience during military service. Video-based education was the preferred method (40.6%), and halitosis prevention and management was the most preferred topic (20.4%). Preferred educational methods did not differ significantly according to age, military rank, educational level, or smoking status (all P > .05). Military rank was significantly associated with perceived adequacy of oral care time (P < .001) and the place of dental treatment (P = .048). Routine dental examinations, dental treatment experience, and oral health education experience showed no significant differences according to participants' general characteristics. Preventive oral health services and education were insufficient among enlisted South Korean Army soldiers. Tailored programs reflecting soldiers' needs and preferred learning methods should be developed and evaluated.

papers.title: Inequitable nutritional impact of India's first COVID-19 lockdown: a national cross-sectional analysis.
papers.abstract: India’s first nationwide COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020 disrupted food systems, healthcare access, and livelihoods, raising concerns about its impact on nutritional outcomes. While the effects of the pandemic on food security have been widely documented, national-level evidence on nutritional status, particularly across economic strata, remains limited. We analyzed data from India’s fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), a national household survey conducted between 2019 and 2021, during which the COVID-19 lockdown occurred. We assessed underweight status (Body Mass Index (BMI) < 18.5 kg/m2) in adults, wasting (weight-for-height z-score < -2) in children under five, and anemia in men, women, and children under five. Outcomes were analyzed by wealth quintile (Q1-Q5). Adjusted prevalences were estimated by marginal standardization. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine associations between lockdown period and outcome prevalence, and concentration indices and curves were applied to assess changes in economic disparities. After adjustment, underweight prevalence among men increased only in the near-poor second quintile (adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) 1.25, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.12–1.40) and declined in the wealthiest, while among women it declined in the wealthier quintiles and overall and was largely unchanged among the poorest. Wasting declined across all wealth quintiles in children, with smaller reductions among the poorest. Anemia declined across all groups. All outcomes remained concentrated in the poorest quintiles in both periods. Concentration indices and curves confirmed widening disparities in underweight and wasting, with smaller or less consistent shifts for anemia. Following India’s first COVID-19 lockdown, undernutrition improved for most groups, but these gains were inequitably distributed: improvements were concentrated among wealthier households while the poorest improved least, and near-poor men experienced a rise in underweight. Anemia declined across all groups but remained highest in the lower wealth quintiles. These estimates should be interpreted with caution, as the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and higher mortality among the most vulnerable during the lockdown may have rendered post-lockdown estimates conservative. These findings point to the need for equity-focused interventions and resilient nutrition systems to protect at-risk populations during and after crises.

The study uses data from the fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) conducted between 2019 and 2021. Adjusted prevalences were estimated using survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression models, and concentration indices and curves were applied to assess economic disparities. papers.title_zh: Inequitable nutritional impact of India's first COVID-19 lockdown: a national cross-sectional analysis.
papers.source_body_en: India’s first nationwide COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020 disrupted food systems, healthcare access, and livelihoods, raising concerns about its impact on nutritional outcomes. While the effects of the pandemic on food security have been widely documented, national-level evidence on nutritional status, particularly across economic strata, remains limited. We analyzed data from India’s fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), a national household survey conducted between 2019 and 2021, during which the COVID-19 lockdown occurred. We assessed underweight status (Body Mass Index (BMI) < 18.5 kg/m2) in adults, wasting (weight-for-height z-score < -2) in children under five, and anemia in men, women, and children under five. Outcomes were analyzed by wealth quintile (Q1-Q5). Adjusted prevalences were estimated by marginal standardization. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine associations between lockdown period and outcome prevalence, and concentration indices and curves were applied to assess changes in economic disparities. After adjustment, underweight prevalence among men increased only in the near-poor second quintile (adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) 1.25, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.12–1.40) and declined in the wealthiest, while among women it declined in the wealthier quintiles and overall and was largely unchanged among the poorest. Wasting declined across all wealth quintiles in children, with smaller reductions among the poorest. Anemia declined across all groups. All outcomes remained concentrated in the poorest quintiles in both periods. Concentration indices and curves confirmed widening disparities in underweight and wasting, with smaller or less consistent shifts for anemia. Following India’s first COVID-19 lockdown, undernutrition improved for most groups, but these gains were inequitably distributed: improvements were concentrated among wealthier households while the poorest improved least, and near-poor men experienced a rise in underweight. Anemia declined across all groups but remained highest in the lower wealth quintiles. These estimates should be interpreted with caution, as the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and higher mortality among the most vulnerable during the lockdown may have rendered post-lockdown estimates conservative. These findings point to the need for equity-focused interventions and resilient nutrition systems to protect at-risk populations during and after crises.

papers.title: Depressive Symptoms among Older Adults with Rheumatoid Arthritis during the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Repeated Cross-sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background To compare the prevalence of depressive symptoms among older adults with and without rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in 2019 and 2022 using large-scale population-based data.Methods This repeated cross-sectional study used data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study 2019 and 2022. A questionnaire was mailed to community-dwelling adults aged ≥65 years, identifying patients with RA undergoing treatment using self-reported information. Depressive symptoms were defined as a Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) score ≥5. Multivariable logistic regression included an interaction term (RA × survey year) to assess whether the association between RA and depressive symptoms differed by year, adjusting for sociodemographic, health, and lifestyle factors.Results The number of participants with and without RA were 433 and 16,958 in 2019 and 472 and 16,881 in 2022 (total: 34,744). From 2019 to 2022, depressive symptoms increased among those with RA (35.5% to 40.4%), but changed minimally among those without RA (25.6% to 26.2%). The RA × year interaction was positive (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.02-1.83; P = 0.036), indicating a greater increase in depressive symptoms among older adults with RA than among non-RA peers. Exploratory stratified analyses showed significant RA-by-year interactions among participants aged ≥75 years, those living alone or unmarried, those with lower educational attainment, never-smokers, and urban residents.Conclusions The difference in depressive symptoms between older adults with and without RA was greater in 2022 than that in 2019. Public health and clinical strategies that incorporate mental health and social support should be considered for vulnerable older adults with RA.

papers.title: Persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection in SCID rats reflects immune vulnerability of the upper airway and trachea
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In immunocompromised patients, persistent severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection carries the risk of prolonged viral shedding and emergence of new variants. To reproduce the key features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and evaluate its transmissibility, mouse-passaged SARS-CoV-2 was administered intranasally to severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) rats deficient in Rag2 and Il2rg genes. The virus replicated in SCID rats for at least 6 weeks without causing severe symptoms. The main replication sites were the nasal cavity and trachea, and replicating viruses were barely detectable in the lungs. Infected areas within the nasal cavity and trachea showed minimal infiltration of neutrophils and M2 macrophages; however, a strong inflammatory response was observed in the lungs. Serial sequencing of the viral genome revealed accumulation of persistent mutations, predominantly in regions encoding nonstructural proteins. The persistently shed virus retained its infectivity, enabling its transmission to uninfected SCID rats. This model provides new insights into the immunological and tissue-associated features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and offers a practical research platform for developing therapeutic interventions. IMPORTANCE Persistent severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection in immunocompromised individuals promotes viral evolution and ongoing transmission, yet mechanistic studies have been limited by the absence of appropriate animal models. Existing mouse systems do not support longitudinal sampling or evaluate transmission, leaving critical questions unanswered. We established an SCID rat model that enables repeated noninvasive sampling from the same individuals, allowing longitudinal analysis of viral dynamics during prolonged infection. This approach revealed the emergence, disappearance, and fixation of viral mutations over time. Persistently infected rats also retained infectious and transmitted virus to naïve SCID rats, providing experimental evidence that prolonged infection preserves the transmission potential in this model. Persistent viral replication localized to the nasal cavity and trachea may be relevant to the upper-airway persistence reported in some immunocompromised patients. By capturing selected features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection under profoundly immunodeficient conditions, this model provides a valuable platform for investigating viral persistence, evolution, and transmission.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection in immunocompromised individuals by developing an SCID rat model. This model was needed to evaluate the transmissibility and viral evolution during prolonged infection, as existing mouse systems lacked the necessary features.
analysis.study_design_and_population: SCID rats deficient in Rag2 and Il2rg genes were used to study persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection. The virus was administered intranasally, and the model allowed repeated noninvasive sampling from the same individuals over 6 weeks.
analysis.methods: SCID rats were infected with mouse-passaged SARS-CoV-2. Viral replication was monitored in the nasal cavity, trachea, and lungs. Serial sequencing of the viral genome revealed persistent mutations, and the virus retained its infectivity, enabling transmission to uninfected SCID rats.
analysis.main_results: SARS-CoV-2 replicated in the nasal cavity and trachea without causing severe symptoms. The virus accumulated mutations predominantly in nonstructural proteins. Infected areas showed minimal immune cell infiltration but a strong inflammatory response in the lungs. The persistently shed virus retained infectivity and could transmit to uninfected SCID rats.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provided new insights into the immunological and tissue-associated features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection, offering a practical research platform for developing therapeutic interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The model captures selected features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection under profoundly immunodeficient conditions, providing valuable insights for investigating viral persistence, evolution, and transmission.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study design limitations include the use of SCID rats, which may not fully represent human immunocompromised conditions. The model provides a valuable platform but does not address all aspects of human infection.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在通过开发 SCID 大鼠模型来了解免疫功能低下个体的持续 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染。由于现有的小鼠系统缺乏必要的特征,因此需要该模型来评估长期感染期间的传播性和病毒 进化。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用 Rag2 和 Il2rg 基因缺陷的 SCID 大鼠来研究持续性 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染。该病毒通过鼻内给药,该模型允许在 6 周内对同一个体重复进行无创采样。
elements_zh.methods: SCID 大鼠被小鼠传代的 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染。在鼻腔、气管和肺部监测病毒复制。病毒 基因组 的系列测序揭示了持久的 突变,并且该病毒保留了其感染性,使 传播 能够作用于未感染的 SCID 大鼠。
elements_zh.main_results: 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 在鼻腔和气管中复制,但没有引起严重症状。该病毒主要在非结构蛋白中积累 突变。感染区域显示出最小的免疫细胞浸润,但肺部出现强烈的炎症反应。持续散发的病毒保留了感染性,并且可以传播给未感染的 SCID 大鼠。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究为持续性 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染的免疫学和组织相关特征提供了新的见解,为开发治疗干预措施提供了实用的研究平台。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该模型捕获了严重免疫缺陷条件下持续性 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染的选定特征,为研究病毒持续性、进化 和 传播 提供了宝贵的见解。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究设计的局限性包括使用 SCID 大鼠,它可能无法完全代表人类免疫功能低下的情况。该模型提供了一个有价值的平台,但并未解决人类感染的所有方面。

papers.source_body_en: ABSTRACT In immunocompromised patients, persistent severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection carries the risk of prolonged viral shedding and emergence of new variants. To reproduce the key features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and evaluate its transmissibility, mouse-passaged SARS-CoV-2 was administered intranasally to severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) rats deficient in Rag2 and Il2rg genes. The virus replicated in SCID rats for at least 6 weeks without causing severe symptoms. The main replication sites were the nasal cavity and trachea, and replicating viruses were barely detectable in the lungs. Infected areas within the nasal cavity and trachea showed minimal infiltration of neutrophils and M2 macrophages; however, a strong inflammatory response was observed in the lungs. Serial sequencing of the viral genome revealed accumulation of persistent mutations, predominantly in regions encoding nonstructural proteins. The persistently shed virus retained its infectivity, enabling its transmission to uninfected SCID rats. This model provides new insights into the immunological and tissue-associated features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and offers a practical research platform for developing therapeutic interventions. IMPORTANCE Persistent severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection in immunocompromised individuals promotes viral evolution and ongoing transmission, yet mechanistic studies have been limited by the absence of appropriate animal models. Existing mouse systems do not support longitudinal sampling or evaluate transmission, leaving critical questions unanswered. We established an SCID rat model that enables repeated noninvasive sampling from the same individuals, allowing longitudinal analysis of viral dynamics during prolonged infection. This approach revealed the emergence, disappearance, and fixation of viral mutations over time. Persistently infected rats also retained infectious and transmitted virus to naïve SCID rats, providing experimental evidence that prolonged infection preserves the transmission potential in this model. Persistent viral replication localized to the nasal cavity and trachea may be relevant to the upper-airway persistence reported in some immunocompromised patients. By capturing selected features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection under profoundly immunodeficient conditions, this model provides a valuable platform for investigating viral persistence, evolution, and transmission.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在通过开发 SCID 大鼠模型来了解免疫功能低下个体的持续 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染。由于现有的小鼠系统缺乏必要的特征,因此需要该模型来评估长期感染期间的传播性和病毒 进化。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用 Rag2 和 Il2rg 基因缺陷的 SCID 大鼠来研究持续性 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染。该病毒通过鼻内给药,该模型允许在 6 周内对同一个体重复进行无创采样。
analysis_zh.methods: SCID 大鼠被小鼠传代的 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染。在鼻腔、气管和肺部监测病毒复制。病毒 基因组 的系列测序揭示了持久的 突变,并且该病毒保留了其感染性,使 传播 能够作用于未感染的 SCID 大鼠。
analysis_zh.main_results: 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 在鼻腔和气管中复制,但没有引起严重症状。该病毒主要在非结构蛋白中积累 突变。感染区域显示出最小的免疫细胞浸润,但肺部出现强烈的炎症反应。持续散发的病毒保留了感染性,并且可以传播给未感染的 SCID 大鼠。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究为持续性 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染的免疫学和组织相关特征提供了新的见解,为开发治疗干预措施提供了实用的研究平台。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该模型捕获了严重免疫缺陷条件下持续性 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染的选定特征,为研究病毒持续性、进化 和 传播 提供了宝贵的见解。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究设计的局限性包括使用 SCID 大鼠,它可能无法完全代表人类免疫功能低下的情况。该模型提供了一个有价值的平台,但并未解决人类感染的所有方面。

papers.title: A moving target: non-stationary selection governs unsupervised prediction of viral fitness
papers.abstract: Anticipating how mutations change viral fitness is central to genomic surveillance and vaccine design, yet the supervised phenotype data behind the most accurate variant-effect predictors are unavailable for most emerging pathogens. We ask how far label-free scoring can go using only sequences, their evolutionary history, and structure. We assemble a modular, fully unsupervised pipeline that estimates a few interpretable terms (intrinsic replicative fitness, antigenic escape, and realized growth), and that lets each term be produced by more than one estimator, so the estimator itself becomes a testable modeling choice. Benchmarking the intrinsic term on 21 viral deep-mutational-scanning assays from ProteinGym, we find that a 650-million-parameter single-sequence protein language model predicts viral mutational fitness weakly and heterogeneously (mean Spearman 0.15 ), whereas a trivial site-independent alignment model more than doubles it ( 0.39 , better on 17 of 21 assays), with the largest gains on the antigenic surface proteins where the language model fails. Yet the ordering reverses across 186 non-viral ProteinGym assays, where the language model instead exceeds the alignment model, localizing the weakness to viral families under-represented in the model's training data. Alignment-conditioned language models (MSA Transformer, Tranception) recover this accuracy but do not clearly exceed the simple alignment, so the decisive feature is the family alignment, not model scale or architecture. Our central result is evolutionary. Using dated samples of SARS-CoV-2 spike and influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin, we show that the epoch of the alignment is itself a leading, virus-specific determinant of accuracy. This traces to non-stationary selection: the site-specific amino-acid preferences drift over time, abruptly for spike at the emergence of Omicron and gradually for H3N2 hemagglutinin. A phylogenetic mutation-selection estimator does not match the far cheaper alignment model, falling significantly below it on matched data. Unsupervised viral fitness prediction is, then, as much an evolutionary problem as a modeling one.

papers.title_zh: 移动目标:非固定选择控制病毒适应度的无监督预测
papers.source_body_en: Anticipating how mutations change viral fitness is central to genomic surveillance and vaccine design, yet the supervised phenotype data behind the most accurate variant-effect predictors are unavailable for most emerging pathogens. We ask how far label-free scoring can go using only sequences, their evolutionary history, and structure. We assemble a modular, fully unsupervised pipeline that estimates a few interpretable terms (intrinsic replicative fitness, antigenic escape, and realized growth), and that lets each term be produced by more than one estimator, so the estimator itself becomes a testable modeling choice. Benchmarking the intrinsic term on 21 viral deep-mutational-scanning assays from ProteinGym, we find that a 650-million-parameter single-sequence protein language model predicts viral mutational fitness weakly and heterogeneously (mean Spearman 0.15 ), whereas a trivial site-independent alignment model more than doubles it ( 0.39 , better on 17 of 21 assays), with the largest gains on the antigenic surface proteins where the language model fails. Yet the ordering reverses across 186 non-viral ProteinGym assays, where the language model instead exceeds the alignment model, localizing the weakness to viral families under-represented in the model's training data. Alignment-conditioned language models (MSA Transformer, Tranception) recover this accuracy but do not clearly exceed the simple alignment, so the decisive feature is the family alignment, not model scale or architecture. Our central result is evolutionary. Using dated samples of SARS-CoV-2 spike and influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin, we show that the epoch of the alignment is itself a leading, virus-specific determinant of accuracy. This traces to non-stationary selection: the site-specific amino-acid preferences drift over time, abruptly for spike at the emergence of Omicron and gradually for H3N2 hemagglutinin. A phylogenetic mutation-selection estimator does not match the far cheaper alignment model, falling significantly below it on matched data. Unsupervised viral fitness prediction is, then, as much an evolutionary problem as a modeling one.

papers.title: Essential work, unequal places: Neighborhood characteristics of the essential workforce in the United States during the COVID-19 pandemic.
papers.abstract: Introduction At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, more than 55 million U.S. workers continued providing "essential" services crucial to public health, safety, and economic stability, even as large segments of the workforce sheltered at home. Despite the central role these workers played in safeguarding the economy and the greater American public, little is known about the neighborhood environments in which essential workers lived and how well these communities were equipped to support the health and well-being of essential workers during the pandemic. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to describe the social and physical characteristics of U.S. neighborhoods with varying concentrations of essential workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods We linked data from the National Neighborhood Data Archive (NaNDA) with American Community Survey (ACS) 2016-2020 estimates to identify the residential concentration of essential workers across U.S. Neighborhoods were categorized into quintiles based on the proportion of essential workers. We examined access to key neighborhood resources relevant to pandemic resilience, including food outlets, health care facilities, and parks/green space. We summarized characteristics using descriptive statistics and heatmaps. Differences between the highest (Q5) and lowest (Q1) quintiles were assessed using Welch's two-sample t-tests. Results Neighborhoods with higher concentrations of essential workers had greater access to grocery stores but significantly less access to health care facilities and parks/green space compared with neighborhoods with fewer essential workers. These disparities highlight uneven community support for those workers required to continue in-person work during a national public health emergency. Conclusion Using nationwide neighborhood and census-tract data, we found that neighborhoods with a high proportion of essential workers generally had better access to food stores but substantially lower access to health care and parks/green space. Recognizing these uneven community conditions is critical for strengthening preparedness efforts and ensuring that neighborhoods are better equipped to support the essential workforce during future disasters and public health crises.

analysis_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The study utilized data from the National Neighborhood Data Archive (NaNDA) and American Community Survey (ACS) 2016-2020 estimates. papers.source_body_en: Introduction At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, more than 55 million U.S. workers continued providing "essential" services crucial to public health, safety, and economic stability, even as large segments of the workforce sheltered at home. Despite the central role these workers played in safeguarding the economy and the greater American public, little is known about the neighborhood environments in which essential workers lived and how well these communities were equipped to support the health and well-being of essential workers during the pandemic. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to describe the social and physical characteristics of U.S. neighborhoods with varying concentrations of essential workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods We linked data from the National Neighborhood Data Archive (NaNDA) with American Community Survey (ACS) 2016-2020 estimates to identify the residential concentration of essential workers across U.S. Neighborhoods were categorized into quintiles based on the proportion of essential workers. We examined access to key neighborhood resources relevant to pandemic resilience, including food outlets, health care facilities, and parks/green space. We summarized characteristics using descriptive statistics and heatmaps. Differences between the highest (Q5) and lowest (Q1) quintiles were assessed using Welch's two-sample t-tests. Results Neighborhoods with higher concentrations of essential workers had greater access to grocery stores but significantly less access to health care facilities and parks/green space compared with neighborhoods with fewer essential workers. These disparities highlight uneven community support for those workers required to continue in-person work during a national public health emergency. Conclusion Using nationwide neighborhood and census-tract data, we found that neighborhoods with a high proportion of essential workers generally had better access to food stores but substantially lower access to health care and parks/green space. Recognizing these uneven community conditions is critical for strengthening preparedness efforts and ensuring that neighborhoods are better equipped to support the essential workforce during future disasters and public health crises.

papers.title: Diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 Infection Using Immunoassays: Antigen/Antibody-Based Tests
papers.abstract: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-induced global pandemic, caused by coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), has taken a toll on millions of lives worldwide. Hence, there is an increasing need for accurate disease diagnosis to prevent rapid transmission and provide immediate treatment to patients having mild to severe symptoms of COVID-19 on an urgent basis. Immunoassays are among the several developed techniques for COVID-19 diagnosis. These are generally biochemical tests designed to identify the presence and level of a SARS-CoV-2-specific biomarker employing either antigens (Ags) or antibodies (Abs). Immunoassays rely on a competitive affinity reaction between the target immunological biomarker (Ag/Ab) and other (bio)molecules present in a patient’s sample for the limited binding sites on the immobilised capture molecule (Ab/Ag). Unlike conventional immunoassays, including quantitative/semi-quantitative serology tests that detect circulating anti-SARS-CoV-2 Abs using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and/or chemiluminescent immunoassay (ChLIA) techniques, rapid immunoassays, or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), are qualitative, simple-to-use assays that utilise an immunochromatographic (lateral flow) test format. Moreover, such tests can be conducted at or near the point of care (PoC) without requiring any high-throughput laboratory infrastructure. Based on the mechanism of detection, SARS-CoV-2 RDTs can be broadly classified into two types, namely (1) Ag tests, which directly identify the SARS-CoV-2 viral Ag(s), and (2) Ab tests that identify one or more variants of antiviral Abs secreted by the host immune system in response to viral infection. Although effective, both techniques have certain limitations. New developments in existing colourimetric lateral flow immunoassays (LFIAs) are underway to address these issues and challenges. Ag-detecting RDTs (Ag-RDTs) are expected to significantly broaden the testing domain, enabling more precise viral load estimation, cost-effective treatment for infected persons, and the formulation of adequate prophylactic measures. In contrast, serology tests [including Ab-detecting RDTs (Ab-RDTs)] could be used for serosurveillance of patients recovered from COVID-19.

papers.title: Correction: Violence and abuse towards staff by patients and the public in general practice since COVID-19: findings from an online survey.
papers.abstract: Background Professionals in general practice (family medicine) experience more violence and abuse by patients and the public than in other healthcare settings. There is limited research on such experiences among non-clinical staff, and no direct comparisons between staff groups in general practice. Aim To explore the following: the extent of violence and abuse from patients or the public towards general practice staff between 2020 and 2023; staff correlates and environmental correlates for violence and abuse; and potential impacts of violence and abuse regarding staff feeling of safety and support at work. Design & setting An online survey of general practice staff was conducted across England between 11 July 2023 and 30 November 2023. Method The survey questions covered demographics, physical violence and threats, verbal abuse, harassment, and inappropriate sexual behaviours experienced or witnessed between 2020 and 2023. It asked whether participants felt safe and supported at work. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare binary outcomes and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used for categorical outcomes. Results Participants ( n = 1152, 44.0% clinical, 56.0% non-clinical) were aged 21-75 years (mean = 47.3 years, standard deviation [SD] = 11.1). Overall, 93.7% reported experiencing any form of violence or abuse, with 92.3% reporting verbal abuse, 47.7% reporting physical violence or threats, 60.5% reporting feeling harassed, and 23.7% reporting inappropriate sexual behaviours. Additionally, 22.3% of staff felt unsafe but only 57.1% felt supported at work. Non-clinical, younger, or less experienced staff and those in urban and deprived areas experience more violence and abuse. Those experiencing it more frequently felt less safe and supported. Conclusions Violence and abuse from patients and the public towards general practice staff may be prevalent and increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. Those at greater risk require more organisational support.

elements_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on an online survey conducted across England between 11 July 2023 and 30 November 2023. The survey questions covered demographics, physical violence and threats, verbal abuse, harassment, and inappropriate sexual behaviours experienced or witnessed between 2020 and 2023. Statistical methods included Mann-Whitney U tests for binary outcomes and Kruskal-Wallis tests for categorical outcomes.
elements_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that violence and abuse from patients and the public towards general practice staff may be prevalent and increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. It also highlights that non-clinical, younger, or less experienced staff and those in urban and deprived areas experience more violence and abuse.
elements_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that there is limited research on such experiences among non-clinical staff and no direct comparisons between staff groups in general practice. Additionally, the study does not provide detailed information on the specific mechanisms or contexts of the violence and abuse.
elements_en.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that those at greater risk require more organisational support. It also implies the need for further research to better understand the specific mechanisms and contexts of violence and abuse, as well as to develop targeted interventions.

papers.title_zh: Correction: Violence and abuse towards staff by patients and the public in general practice since COVID-19: findings from an online survey.
papers.source_body_en: Background Professionals in general practice (family medicine) experience more violence and abuse by patients and the public than in other healthcare settings. There is limited research on such experiences among non-clinical staff, and no direct comparisons between staff groups in general practice. Aim To explore the following: the extent of violence and abuse from patients or the public towards general practice staff between 2020 and 2023; staff correlates and environmental correlates for violence and abuse; and potential impacts of violence and abuse regarding staff feeling of safety and support at work. Design & setting An online survey of general practice staff was conducted across England between 11 July 2023 and 30 November 2023. Method The survey questions covered demographics, physical violence and threats, verbal abuse, harassment, and inappropriate sexual behaviours experienced or witnessed between 2020 and 2023. It asked whether participants felt safe and supported at work. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare binary outcomes and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used for categorical outcomes. Results Participants ( n = 1152, 44.0% clinical, 56.0% non-clinical) were aged 21-75 years (mean = 47.3 years, standard deviation [SD] = 11.1). Overall, 93.7% reported experiencing any form of violence or abuse, with 92.3% reporting verbal abuse, 47.7% reporting physical violence or threats, 60.5% reporting feeling harassed, and 23.7% reporting inappropriate sexual behaviours. Additionally, 22.3% of staff felt unsafe but only 57.1% felt supported at work. Non-clinical, younger, or less experienced staff and those in urban and deprived areas experience more violence and abuse. Those experiencing it more frequently felt less safe and supported. Conclusions Violence and abuse from patients and the public towards general practice staff may be prevalent and increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. Those at greater risk require more organisational support.

papers.title: An intersectionality-based policy analysis of COVID-19 measures and women informal food vendors in Kisumu, Kenya.
papers.abstract: Introduction Women working as informal food vendors in Kisumu faced precarious work conditions that worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite playing a vital role in urban household food security, they were excluded from policy decisions, which were largely confined to technical experts and national government officials. Methods Using the Intersectionality-Based Policy Analysis (IBPA) framework, this study examined the engagement of women informal food vendors and the disparities in COVID-19 control policies. Between July 10, 2024, and October 15, 2024, we conducted a qualitative study using key informant interviews (n = 20), in-depth interviews (n = 20), four focus group discussions (n = 40; 10 participants each), and a purposive review of four policy documents. Participants were recruited via purposive sampling in collaboration with Pamoja Community Based Organisation, and data were analyzed thematically guided by the IBPA principles. Results The findings indicate that excluding women vendors from decision-making led to gender-insensitive policies that worsened existing inequalities by overlooking the vendors' diverse social identities. Furthermore, inconsistent policy implementation increased gender-based vulnerabilities, leaving these women exposed to harassment, extortion, and physical assault. Discussion To prepare for future emergencies, governments must establish inclusive, gender-responsive policy frameworks that prioritize the perspectives of informal food vendors, thereby safeguarding sustainable urban food systems. Specifically, municipal, county, and national authorities should create consultative mechanisms to ensure women informal food vendors actively participate in decision-making processes. Such integration will foster gender-sensitive policy development and keep vendors' lived experiences central to urban food governance. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the value of applying an intersectional policy analysis framework to health research, advancing equity and social justice by strengthening the participation of marginalized groups in emergency response and regulatory planning.

papers.title: Breadth of ACE2 receptor usage predicts host range and antigenic relatedness across bat sarbecoviruses
papers.abstract: Sarbecoviruses interact with their receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), via the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of Spike, the immunodominant target for neutralising antibodies. Understanding the interplay and correlation between ACE2-determined host range and antigenicity is vitally important for understanding the zoonotic potential of related bat sarbecoviruses. Using binding assays, pseudotype-entry assays and a diverse panel of mammalian ACE2 proteins, we examined the host range and related antigenicity of multiple bat coronaviruses. Broad bat ACE2 usage (a generalist phenotype) was most common in clade 1 sarbecoviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and the BANAL isolates from Laos. In contrast, clade 3 (e.g., RhGB07) and 5 (e.g., Rc-o319) sarbecoviruses exhibited more restricted ACE2 usage (a specialist phenotype). A novel structure for RhGB07 Spike further helped to identify RBD residues associated with this receptor specialism. Interestingly, the generalist phenotypes were largely maintained with more diverse mammalian receptor libraries, including human, non-human primate, livestock, rodent ACE2 and potential intermediate reservoir hosts (e.g., civet, racoon dog, pangolin), while specialists, like RhGB07, exhibited wider phenotypic diversity. The impact of SARS-CoV-2's continued evolution in humans was also examined, identifying an expanding and/or shifting pattern of generalism for variants, especially Omicron and its sub-lineages. Furthermore, we compared and correlated these entry phenotypes with antigenicity using sera from SARS-CoV-2 convalescent individuals. Clade 1 viruses, phylogenetically related to SARS-CoV-2, were antigenically the most similar, with robust evidence for cross-neutralisation; however, there was still evidence for limited cross-neutralisation across the entire sub-genus. Finally, using monoclonal antibodies, derived from COVID-19 vaccinees with breakthrough infections, we pin-pointed the antibody epitope classes responsible for wider neutralisation. Our research indicates that generalist ACE2-using sarbecoviruses are phylogenetically and antigenically related to SARS-CoV-2.

It also included analysis of SARS-CoV-2 variants and compared entry phenotypes with antigenicity using sera from SARS-CoV-2 convalescent individuals.
analysis.methods: The researchers conducted binding assays, pseudotype-entry assays, and used a diverse panel of mammalian ACE2 proteins to assess host range and antigenicity. They also employed monoclonal antibodies from vaccinees with breakthrough infections to identify epitopes responsible for neutralisation.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the zoonotic potential of related bat sarbecoviruses and highlight the importance of monitoring generalist phenotypes, especially in the context of SARS-CoV-2's continued evolution in humans.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only evidence, which may limit the depth of analysis. However, the results are supported by multiple assays and comparisons with SARS-CoV-2, indicating moderate confidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the relationship between ACE2 receptor usage and antigenic relatedness among bat sarbecoviruses, focusing on their zoonotic potential. Using binding assays, pseudotype-entry assays, and sera from SARS-CoV-2 convalescents, the researchers found that clade 1 viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and BANAL isolates, exhibit broad ACE2 usage, while clade 3 and 5 viruses show more restricted usage. A novel structure for RhGB07 Spike helped identify RBD residues linked to its receptor specialism. The study also observed expanding generalism in SARS-CoV-2 variants, particularly Omicron sub-lineages. These findings suggest that generalist ACE2-using sarbecoviruses are phylogenetically and antigenically related to SARS-CoV-2, which has implications for understanding viral evolution and host range. However, the evidence is based on abstract-only data, which may limit the depth of analysis, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

papers.title_zh: ACE2 受体使用的广度可预测蝙蝠 sarbecovirus 的 宿主 范围和抗原相关性
papers.source_body_en: Sarbecoviruses interact with their receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), via the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of Spike, the immunodominant target for neutralising antibodies. Understanding the interplay and correlation between ACE2-determined host range and antigenicity is vitally important for understanding the zoonotic potential of related bat sarbecoviruses. Using binding assays, pseudotype-entry assays and a diverse panel of mammalian ACE2 proteins, we examined the host range and related antigenicity of multiple bat coronaviruses. Broad bat ACE2 usage (a generalist phenotype) was most common in clade 1 sarbecoviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and the BANAL isolates from Laos. In contrast, clade 3 (e.g., RhGB07) and 5 (e.g., Rc-o319) sarbecoviruses exhibited more restricted ACE2 usage (a specialist phenotype). A novel structure for RhGB07 Spike further helped to identify RBD residues associated with this receptor specialism. Interestingly, the generalist phenotypes were largely maintained with more diverse mammalian receptor libraries, including human, non-human primate, livestock, rodent ACE2 and potential intermediate reservoir hosts (e.g., civet, racoon dog, pangolin), while specialists, like RhGB07, exhibited wider phenotypic diversity. The impact of SARS-CoV-2's continued evolution in humans was also examined, identifying an expanding and/or shifting pattern of generalism for variants, especially Omicron and its sub-lineages. Furthermore, we compared and correlated these entry phenotypes with antigenicity using sera from SARS-CoV-2 convalescent individuals. Clade 1 viruses, phylogenetically related to SARS-CoV-2, were antigenically the most similar, with robust evidence for cross-neutralisation; however, there was still evidence for limited cross-neutralisation across the entire sub-genus. Finally, using monoclonal antibodies, derived from COVID-19 vaccinees with breakthrough infections, we pin-pointed the antibody epitope classes responsible for wider neutralisation. Our research indicates that generalist ACE2-using sarbecoviruses are phylogenetically and antigenically related to SARS-CoV-2.
papers.abstract_zh: Sarbecoviruses 通过 Spike 的受体结合域 (RBD) 与其受体血管紧张素转换酶 2 (ACE2) 相互作用,Spike 是中和抗体的免疫显性靶点。了解 ACE2 确定的 宿主 范围与抗原性之间的相互作用和相关性对于了解相关蝙蝠 sarbecovirus 的人畜共患潜力至关重要。使用结合测定、假型输入测定和多种哺乳动物 ACE2 蛋白,我们检查了多种蝙蝠冠状病毒的 宿主 范围和相关抗原性。阔蝙蝠 ACE2 使用(通才表型)在进化枝 1 sarbecoviruses 中最常见,包括 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 和来自老挝的 BANAL 分离株。相比之下,进化枝 3(例如,RhGB07)和 5(例如,Rc-o319)sarbecoviruses 表现出更严格的 ACE2 使用(特殊表型)。RhGB07 Spike 的新颖结构进一步有助于识别与这种受体特殊性相关的 RBD 残基。有趣的是,通才表型在很大程度上维持在更多样化的哺乳动物受体库中,包括人类、非人灵长类动物、牲畜、啮齿动物 ACE2 和潜在的中间体 储存宿主 宿主(例如果子狸、貉、穿山甲),而专才表型(如 RhGB07)则表现出更广泛的表型多样性。还检查了 进化 的持续 进化 对人类的影响,确定了变体(尤其是 Omicron 及其子谱系)的扩展和/或转变的普遍性模式。此外,我们使用 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 恢复期个体的血清对这些进入表型与抗原性进行了比较和关联。进化枝 1 病毒在系统发育上与 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 相关,在抗原上最相似,有交叉中和作用的有力证据;然而,仍然有证据表明整个亚属的交叉中和作用有限。最后,使用源自具有突破性感染的 新型冠状病毒感染 疫苗 的单克隆抗体,我们精确定位了负责更广泛中和的抗体表位类别。我们的研究表明,使用 ACE2 的多面性 sarbecoviruses 在系统发育和抗原性上与 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 相关。

Cases Deaths Hospitalizations Vaccines Variants Wastewater Data About More resources More COVID-19 Cases, %%COUNTRY%% WHO will utilize various sources to continue monitoring the COVID-19 epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these statistics at a global level. Please note that statistics do not necessarily reflect the actual number of cases and deaths or the actual number of countries where cases and deaths are occurring, as a number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting. Trends in COVID-19 cases, %%COUNTRY%% Recent COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, July 2023 - present Source: World Health Organization Data may be incomplete for the latest week. Total COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, January 2020 - present Source: World Health Organization Why is COVID-19 data being presented as weekly statistics? A number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting COVID-19 case and death counts to WHO. An outcome of these differences in reporting is that WHO may receive daily data from some countries, while other countries may only report data to WHO once every 14 days. In addition, countries differ in how they choose to report statistics; some countries provide their data attributed to specific dates while others who report less frequently may group data from 7 days into a single statistic attributed to a week in their reporting. As of 25 August 2023, WHO declared that it is no longer necessary for Member States to report daily counts of cases and deaths to WHO and requested strengthening of weekly reporting. Reported data is still available attributed to specific dates (daily data) here as a download. This dashboard presents the same statistics as weekly figures in charts in order to mitigate against the visual misinterpretation of data. Should daily data have been presented here, many countries would show zero counts for multiple consecutive days due in part to the differences in how they choose to report. While weekly intervals do not completely mitigate against this, the approach reduces the risk that some dashboard users might infer zero cases or deaths when lack of data is often due to reporting differences. What do negative counts of cases or deaths mean? All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected by Member States at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections in their reporting. Bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. Last 28 days ‘Last 28 days’ refers to the four preceding most recently complete epidemiological weeks. WHO Regions The World Health Organization (WHO) is divided into six regions with regional offices, each responsible for addressing health challenges and promoting public health within its designated geographical area. These regions serve as administrative units that allow the WHO to tailor its efforts to the specific needs, priorities, and health conditions of member countries within each region. These annually updated classifications help the World Bank and other organizations analyze and understand global economic trends, allocate resources, and design development policies. WHO COVID-19 Dashboard is updated every Tuesday for the period of two full weeks prior. Counts primarily reflect laboratory-confirmed cases and deaths, based upon WHO case definitions; although some departures may exist due to local adaptations. Counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these data at a global level. All data represent date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data are subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals. New case and death counts from the Region of the Americas Starting from the week commencing on 11 September 2023, the source of the data from the Region of the Americas was switched to the aggregated national surveillances, received through the COVID-19, Influenza, RSV and Other Respiratory Viruses program in the Americas. Data have been included retrospectively since 31 July 2023. Rates <0.001 per 100,000 population may be rounded to 0. Health Blogs AstraZeneca Covid-19 Vaccine WHY GETTING VACCINATED AGAINST COVID-19? Covid-19 vaccination greatly reduces the chance of you suffering from Covid-19 disease. No vaccine is 100% effective, however numerous studies have shown 75-85% efficacy of the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine against symptomatic Covid-19 and an impressive 100% efficacy against severe or critical disease and hospitalisations. This means that the few vaccinated people who do get infected have essentially mild to moderate cases of Covid-19 and that your risk of hospitalisation and death because of Covid-19 is nearly eliminated once you are fully vaccinated. Also, vaccinated people who might be infected with the coronavirus have fewer virus particles in their nose and mouth and are less likely to spread it to others. This reduced transmission is important as getting vaccinated now not only protects you, but also limits spreading the virus to loved ones, friends and other people. Reduced transmission is such that, on 13 May 2021, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have released an updated guidance saying that fully vaccinated people (2 weeks after their second dose) no longer need to wear a face mask or respect physical distancing in most settings, whether outdoors or indoors. In addition, recent studies have shown that, after 2 doses, the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine is highly effective at protecting people against specific coronavirus strains (called “variants of concern”) such as the Indian, the Brazilian, the South African and the Kent variants. WHAT IS ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE? Covid-19 disease is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine is made up of another virus (of the adenovirus family) that has been modified to contain the gene for making the Covid-19 virus spike protein. This is a protein on the surface of the virus which the virus needs to enter the body’s cells. HOW DOES ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE WORK? Once it has been given, the vaccine delivers the spike gene into cells in the body. The cells will use the gene to produce the spike protein. The person’s immune system will then recognise this protein as foreign and produce antibodies (by the “B cells”) and activate specific white blood cells (called “T cells”) to attack it. If, later on, the person comes into contact with SARS-CoV-2 virus, their immune system will recognise it and be ready to defend the body against it. AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine does not contain the Covid-19 virus itself and cannot cause Covid-19 disease. The adenovirus in the vaccine cannot reproduce and cannot cause disease. CAN THE COVID-19 VACCINE CAUSE A POSITIVE TEST RESULT FOR THE DISEASE, SUCH AS FOR A PCR OR ANTIGEN TEST? No, the Covid-19 vaccine will not cause a positive test result for a Covid-19 PCR or antigen laboratory test. This is because these tests check for active disease and not whether an individual is immune or not. However, because the Covid-19 vaccine prompts an immune response, vaccinated people usually test positive in an antibody (serology) test that measures Covid-19 immunity in an individual. HOW IS ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE ADMINISTERED? The AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine is injected into a muscle (usually in the upper arm). The vaccine will be given in 2 doses. You will be advised when to return for your second dose. The second dose can be given between 4 and 12 weeks after the first dose. Post-vaccination observation times: 30 minutes: persons with a history of an immediate allergic reaction of any severity to a vaccine or injectable therapy or a history of anaphylaxis due to any cause; 15 minutes: all other persons. HOW LONG DOES PROTECTION FROM ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE LAST? Covid-19 vaccination offers good protection within 2 to 3 weeks of the first dose. It takes 2 weeks after getting the second dose to have the best protection, therefore it’s essential to get both doses to protect yourself against Covid-19. It is not currently known how long the protection given by AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine lasts, however experts believe that immunity from Covid-19 vaccines will last longer than six months and most probably at least longer than one year. CAN CHILDREN BE VACCINATED WITH ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE? AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine is currently only authorised for people aged 18 years and older. Trials are being conducted involving children, and other Covid-19 vaccines are already authorised in several countries for children between 12 and 17-year old. CAN IMMUNOCOMPROMISED PEOPLE BE VACCINATED WITH ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE? Although immunocompromised people (people with weakened immune systems) may not respond as well to the vaccine, there are no particular safety concerns. Immunocompromised people should be vaccinated as they may be at higher risk from Covid-19. CAN PREGNANT OR BREAST-FEEDING WOMEN BE VACCINATED WITH ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE? Pregnant women when vaccinated create antibodies to the virus and pass those to their unborn baby through the placenta. Pregnant people are at increased risk for severe illness from Covid-19. Women with Covid-19 disease are also 2 to 3 times more likely to have their babies early than women without Covid-19 and might be at increased risk of other adverse pregnancy outcomes. Pregnant women with underlying clinical conditions are at even higher risk of suffering serious complications from Covid-19. For these reasons, many countries including the US, the UK, Israel and France recommend that pregnant people get vaccinated and are to be treated as priority cases. The vaccine can be given at any stage during pregnancy. There is no reason to delay a pregnancy after Covid-19 vaccination. Covid-19 vaccines are thought not to be a risk to lactating people or their breastfeeding babies. Actually mothers were shown to pass antibodies to their newborns through breast milk. Therefore, lactating people can receive a Covid-19 vaccine. CAN PEOPLE VACCINATED RECENTLY WITH ANOTHER VACCINE RECEIVE ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE? Covid-19 vaccines and other vaccines may be administered without regard to timing. This includes simultaneous administration of Covid-19 vaccine and other vaccines on the same day, as well as co-administration within 14 days. DO YOU HAVE A BLEEDING DISORDER OR ARE YOU TAKING A BLOOD THINNER? As with all vaccines, Covid-19 vaccine may be given to these patients, if a doctor determines that the patient’s bleeding risk is low enough and the vaccine can be administered intramuscularly with reasonable safety. The following technique for intramuscular vaccination in patients with bleeding disorders or taking blood thinners is recommended: a fine-gauge needle (23-gauge or smaller calibre) should be used for the vaccination, followed by firm pressure on the site, without rubbing, for at least 2 minutes ARE THERE ANY REASONS YOU SHOULD NOT GET THE VACCINE? There are very few people who cannot get the Covid-19 vaccine. The vaccine should not be given to: People who have had a confirmed anaphylactic reaction to any of the ingredients of the vaccine; those who have had a confirmed anaphylactic reaction to a previous dose of the same Covid-19 vaccine. People with a history of serious allergic reaction to food, an identified drug or vaccine, or an insect sting can get any Covid-19 vaccine, as long as they are not known to be allergic to any component of the Covid-19 vaccine. It’s important that you tell the person giving you your vaccine if you have ever had a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis). Are you feeling sick today? There is no evidence that acute illness reduces vaccine efficacy or increases vaccine adverse events. However, as a precaution with moderate or severe acute illness, all vaccines should be delayed until the illness has improved. Mild illnesses (e.g., upper respiratory infections, diarrhoea) are NOT contraindications to vaccination. Do not withhold vaccination if a person is taking antibiotics. Have you received another vaccine in the last 14 days? The Covid-19 vaccine should be administered alone, with a minimum interval of 14 days before or after administration of other vaccines. WHAT ARE THE RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH ASTRAZENECA COVID-19 VACCINE? Like all medicines, vaccines can cause side effects. So far, millions of people have been given the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine and reports of serious side effects, such as allergic reactions and blood clots, have been very rare. No long-term complications have been reported. Most of the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine side effects are mild and short-term (a few days), and not everyone gets them (about 10-20% of people), they include: A sore arm where the needle went in; Feeling tired; A headache; Feeling achy; Nausea; Some people will experience mild flu-like symptoms; Very few people get a high temperature or feel hot or shivery 1 or 2 days after vaccination; An uncommon side effect is swollen glands in the armpit or neck on the same side as the arm where you had the vaccine. This can last for around 10 days, but if it lasts longer see your doctor. Allergic reactions Allergic reactions (hypersensitivity) have been seen in people receiving the vaccine. Cases of anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction) are rare. If you do have a reaction to the vaccine, it usually happens in minutes. Signs of an allergic reaction may include itchy skin rash, shortness of breath and swelling of the face or tongue. Show original Photo by dabun_dabenstein The Complete Record of the COVID-19 Pandemic #12 | October–November 2021: The Silence of 'Record Lows,' 70% Double Vaccination, and the Emergence of the Omicron Variant Tiga 2026年10月3日 17:51 In the previous installment (#11), we followed the situation up to the full lifting of the state of emergency on September 30, after the fifth wave peaked around August 20, leaving behind a record of over 25,000 new daily infections and 2,221 severe cases. Daily life was supposed to be returning. From October to November, Japan's new infections repeatedly hit 'record lows,' and the number of severe cases fell below 200 for the first time in a year. In the final week of November, just as everyone was beginning to say that 'COVID is over,' news broke that shattered the silence: the Omicron variant. These two months contained both the calmest period of the pandemic and the starting gun for the next wave. October: 'Life without a state of emergency' for the first time in about five months, and anxiety over the decline leveling off October began with the state of emergency and priority measures to prevent the spread of disease, which had been in effect intermittently since April 25, fully lifted across the country[d]. It was 'life without a state of emergency' for the first time in about five months. The decline in infections continued, and on October 11, the national count hit 369, a new low for the year. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's advisory board reported on October 13 that the number of new infections per 100,000 people over the previous week was about 4, which was lower than the level before the previous surge, and that all prefectures were below 10 per 100,000. The effective reproduction number was 0.63 nationwide as of September 26. Since late August, it had remained well below 1 for over a month[a]. Requests for restaurants to shorten operating hours, which had remained in some areas after the state of emergency was lifted, were gradually lifted region by region, with Okinawa, the last remaining area, lifting them on October 31[d]. On October 18, the national count hit 232, a new low for the year, and on October 26, the number of severe cases fell to 197, dropping below 200 for the first time in a year since November 8, 2020[d]. However, experts were not celebrating unconditionally. The same advisory board warned that 'following the lifting of the state of emergency measures, there has been a noticeable increase in the number of people staying out at night, and in some regions, the effective reproduction number has risen at times, raising concerns about a slowdown or leveling off in the decline of infection numbers'[a]. In fact, the number of new infections for the week ending October 19 fell 35% from the previous week to 2.67 per 100,000, and 'concerns about the decline leveling off' were being reported[e][f]. Although the numbers were at record lows, the interpretation of those numbers was shifting to the possibility that 'they might not go any lower.' In terms of policy, preparations for the next wave also began. On October 28, a Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare expert panel agreed on a policy to offer a third vaccine dose (booster shot) to 'all citizens who wish to receive it,' starting approximately eight months after the second dose[d]. Furthermore, an event occurred this month that cast doubt on the numbers themselves. On October 29, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government announced that there had been an omission in the infection count from April to October, resulting in an undercount of 4,065 cases. Due to the correction, the number of infections on August 13, the highest in Tokyo, increased by 135 to 5,908[d]. This meant the 'peak' of the fifth wave had become slightly higher in retrospect. On November 1, Johns Hopkins University reported that the global COVID death toll had surpassed 5 million. The containment of the virus was strictly a Japanese phenomenon. November: '86 cases a day' and 'zero deaths,' yet preparations continued The numbers in November looked as if we were watching a different infectious disease. On November 1, there were 86 new infections nationwide. It was the first time the number had fallen below 100 in one year and four months, since June 27, 2020. Tokyo had 9 cases, the first time under 10 in one year and five months, and Osaka had 7, the first time under 10 in one year and four months[d]. On November 7, the number of reported deaths for a single day was zero for the first time in one year and three months, since August 2, 2020[d]. On November 15, the national count hit 79 (7 in Tokyo), a new low for the year, and on November 22, it hit a new low of 50 nationwide. On that day, only Kanagawa had double-digit infections (10), while 35 prefectures had zero[d]. By the end of the month on November 30, there were 132 cases nationwide, 41 severe cases, and 27 prefectures with zero. Tokyo had 21 cases, marking 19 consecutive days of fewer than 30 cases per day, with a seven-day average of 15.0[d]. The number of severe cases in November continued to fall from around 100 to the 40s, and the November 9 advisory board reported that 'the number of severe cases is at its lowest level since last autumn' and 'the number of deaths has fallen below the level before this current surge'[b]. Vaccines supported this silence. The same report stated that more than 70% of the entire population had completed two doses, and about 70% of those aged 12–19 had received at least one dose[b]. The vaccination rate, which had exceeded 50% of the population in mid-September, had increased by more than 10 percentage points over these two months. However, expert warnings became even stronger. 'Although the number of new infections has continued to decline nationwide since November and remains at a very low level, transmission is still ongoing.' 'As we approach the end of the year, with social and economic activities expected to become more active due to annual events such as year-end parties, Christmas, and New Year holidays, it is important to maintain the current low level while keeping an eye on a potential resurgence of infections'[b]. On November 8, the government's subcommittee presented a new way of classifying levels[b]. In the process of moving toward convergence, preparations for the next wave were underway. Society, too, was trying to reclaim its daily life. On November 19, the government approved 'Economic Measures for Overcoming COVID-19 and Pioneering a New Era' at a cabinet meeting[g][h]. The scale of the project was 78.9 trillion yen, with national fiscal spending reaching 55.7 trillion yen, including benefits equivalent to 100,000 yen for those 18 and under, payments of up to 2.5 million yen for businesses with reduced sales, and the resumption of the Go To campaign[i][j][k]. While the budget was intended as an infection control measure, its content was aimed at steering toward a 'with-COVID economy.' November 26: The emergence of a new variable called the 'Omicron variant' The calm ended in the final week of November. On November 24, South Africa first reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) a new lineage of the novel coronavirus, 'B.1.1.529,' which possessed an unprecedented number of mutations[l]. This variant had at least 30 mutations in its spike protein, and infections were spreading rapidly in South Africa at the same time it was detected[m][n]. On November 26, the WHO designated this variant as a 'Variant of Concern (VOC),' the highest level of alert, and named it the 'Omicron variant'[o][p]. There were reports that 'Nu' and 'Xi' were skipped in the Greek alphabet sequence to avoid phonetic associations—an anecdote that was widely covered[q]. The naming itself was a 'signal of alert' to the world. Financial markets reacted immediately. The Nikkei Stock Average fell sharply by 2.53% from the previous day, and in the New York market, the Dow Jones Industrial Average saw a temporary drop of over $1,000[r][s]. It was a global stock market crash. Before the infection itself, the fear of an 'unknown variant' was priced into the market. Japan's response was swift. On November 26, the government strengthened border controls for six countries, including South Africa, and mandated a 10-day quarantine at designated accommodation facilities[d]. On November 27, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida added Mozambique, Malawi, and Zambia, expanding the list to nine countries[d]. On November 29, it was announced that new entry of foreign nationals from all over the world would be suspended in principle for the time being, for about one month. The suspension, including for those who had already been issued visas, took effect from midnight on November 30[t]. The Prime Minister stated, 'I am prepared to take full responsibility for the criticism that I am being too cautious when the situation is still unknown'[u]. Then, on November 30, Chief Cabinet Secretary Matsuno revealed that the Omicron variant had been detected in a man in his 30s who had entered the country from Namibia in southern Africa[[phv]][[phw]]. It was the first confirmation within Japan. On that day, when new daily infections nationwide had dropped to 132, Japan would count the 'first case' of the next wave. Designated by the WHO on November 26 and found in the country on the 30th—this speed itself spoke volumes about the nature of the Omicron variant. Conclusion The two months from October to November were the calmest period of the COVID-19 pandemic if you look only at the numbers. However, looking back, this tranquility was unique in three respects. First, the speed and depth of the decline. New daily infections nationwide fell from the 25,000 range to the 50s, and severe cases dropped from 2,221 to 41. The end of the fifth wave was faster and deeper than expected. Second, it was vaccines that supported this silence. More than 70% of the entire population had completed two doses, and the levels of severe illness and death fell below those seen before the spread of infection[[phb]]. Japan was finally entering a stage where immunity, rather than behavioral restrictions, was suppressing the infection. Third, that tranquility was ended from the outside. The Omicron variant emerged independently of Japan's domestic situation, forcing the borders to close overnight in the form of border control measures. And on November 30, simultaneously with the first domestic confirmation, Japan began the countdown to the next wave. The next installment will cover the start of the third dose, the re-issuance of priority measures to prevent the spread of disease, and the sixth wave in January—the winter when the Omicron variant changed from an 'unknown threat' to a 'real wave.'
