supplementary_news.content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 1-Oct-2026 COVID-19 immunity may help protect against other bat coronaviruses Study identifies links between virus host range and immune recognition Peer-Reviewed Publication The Pirbright Institute Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: A Rhinolophus bat. Photo courtesy of Bernard Agwanda, National Museums of Kenya. view more Credit: Bernard Agwanda, National Museums of Kenya People who recovered from COVID-19 infection or were vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2 are more likely to have immunity to other closely related bat coronaviruses that could have the potential to threaten future human health. In a joint study by The Pirbright Institute and King’s College London (KCL), scientists found bat coronaviruses most likely to infect a wide range of animal species are those most closely related to SARS-CoV-2 and most likely to be recognised by immunity generated through COVID-19 infection. The research, funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (UK Research and Innovation - UKRI), Wellcome, and the Medical Research Council (MRC - part of UKRI), is published today in two companion articles in PLOS Biology. Researchers examined how a diverse group of bat sarbecoviruses - the coronavirus sub-group that includes SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 - interact with ACE2, the cellular receptor used by many coronaviruses to enter host cells. They investigated the ability of these viruses to use ACE2 proteins from a broad range of bat and mammalian species, including humans, livestock, rodents and animals previously proposed as intermediate hosts. The team discovered so-called "generalist" sarbecoviruses, which can use ACE2 receptors from many different species, were largely confined to the same evolutionary group as SARS-CoV-2. Pirbright postdoctoral scientist and lead author, Dr Nazia Thakur, said: "Our findings suggest that the bat coronaviruses currently considered most likely to spill over into humans are also most likely to be recognised by existing COVID-19 immunity. While spillover risk can never be eliminated, widespread exposure to SARS-CoV-2 may have raised the barrier for related viruses to establish themselves in human populations." The team analysed 15 representative bat coronavirus spike proteins using libraries of ACE2 receptors from 34 species. Broad ACE2 usage was a defining feature of viruses closely related to SARS-CoV-2, including the BANAL viruses discovered in Laos. Viruses from other evolutionary groups, including a novel UK bat coronavirus RhGB07, showed more restricted receptor usage. To aid in their analyses the Spike structure of RhGB07 was also resolved by collaborators in Switzerland. The study also investigated how SARS-CoV-2 host range has evolved during the pandemic. Researchers found variants, particularly those within the Omicron lineage acquired mutations in the receptor binding domain which resulted in shifting patterns of ACE2 usage across animal species, highlighting the dynamic relationship between viral evolution and host susceptibility. To understand the implications for human health, the scientists examined blood samples from people who had recovered from COVID-19. Antibodies in these samples successfully neutralised a range of closely related bat coronaviruses. Importantly, researchers also detected lower levels of neutralisation against more distant bat sarbecoviruses, suggesting some degree of broader protection. Katie Doores, Professor of Viral Immunology at KCL, said, “These viruses showed the strongest antigenic similarity to SARS-CoV-2, meaning they were more readily recognised and neutralised by antibodies generated following COVID-19 infection. In contrast, more distantly related bat coronaviruses tended to be "specialists", capable of using ACE2 receptors from only a limited range of hosts.” Further experiments at KCL and Pirbright identified several monoclonal antibodies capable of recognising a remarkably diverse range of sarbecoviruses. The second companion article identified where these monoclonal antibodies bind, highlighting conserved regions of the coronavirus spike protein, and offering important clues for the development of next-generation vaccines and therapeutics. Dr Dalan Bailey, head of Pirbright’s Viral Glycoproteins group, added: "One of the encouraging findings was evidence of cross-neutralisation of even some of the more distantly related bat coronaviruses. This suggests that broadly protective, pan-sarbecovirus vaccines or therapeutics may be achievable." The work highlights the importance of understanding virus host range, receptor usage and immune recognition together rather than in isolation. By identifying characteristics that distinguish higher-risk viruses from those less likely to spill over into humans, researchers hope to strengthen global pandemic preparedness efforts. Stand-Alone Drug Plan Enrollees Will See Modest Premium Increases for 2027, But Others Could Pay Much More If They Don’t Switch Plans Oct 2, 2026 Issue Brief This brief analyzes the Medicare Part D stand-alone prescription drug plan (PDP) market for 2027. The analysis shows that there will be a modest reduction in the number of PDPs for 2027, along with modest premium increases less than $10 per month for many enrollees, but much larger monthly premium increases of $50 or more for others if they don’t change plans. Medicare 101 Oct 1, 2026 Feature This Health Policy 101 chapter explores Medicare, a federal health insurance program covering more than 68 million people, established in 1965 for people age 65 or older and later expanded to cover people under age 65 with long-term disabilities. In addition to detailing Medicare eligibility, coverage, and spending, the chapter examines the increased role of private plans in providing benefits and the financing challenges posed by increasing health care costs and an aging population. Status of State Medicaid Expansion Decisions Oct 1, 2026 Interactive This page displays an interactive map of the current status of state decisions on the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion. Additional Medicaid expansion resources are listed (with links) below the map. The Average Medicare Beneficiary has 28 Medicare Advantage Prescription Drug Plan Options for 2027 Oct 1, 2026 Issue Brief The average Medicare beneficiary will have 28 Medicare Advantage prescription drug (MA_PD) plans available for general enrollment in 2027. The number of plans varies widely across states. How Is The Federal Government Counting Measles Deaths? Oct 1, 2026 Policy Watch Recently Secretary of HHS Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., changed how the federal government tracks deaths in its official measles tally, after Pennsylvania reported four deaths. This Policy Watch reviews the two roles, strengths, and weaknesses of the two public health surveillance systems at the center of this change: the Nationally Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) and the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS). What Are the Recent Trends in Health Sector Employment Sep 30, 2026 Issue Brief Health care employment continues to grow even as hiring across other sectors has plateaued. The health sector added nearly 379,000 jobs over the past year, a 2% increase, compared with just 0.2% growth in other non-farm employment, with outpatient care among the fastest-growing health care settings. Medicaid Waiver Tracker: Approved and Pending Section 1115 Waivers by State Sep 30, 2026 Tracker Section 1115 Medicaid waivers can allow states to test new approaches in Medicaid that differ from what is required by federal law. This page tracks approved and pending waiver provisions (including expansions and restrictions) related to eligibility, benefits, and social determinants of health and other delivery system reforms. The Legal and Policy Landscape of Crisis Pregnancy Centers Sep 30, 2026 Issue Brief This brief examines the legal status of Crisis Pregnancy Centers, attempts to regulate them, and future efforts to expand their footprints as they gain more recognition and funding from local, state, and federal programs. Early Medicaid Work Requirement Insights From Nebraska Sep 29, 2026 Policy Watch This brief describes the verification process for Medicaid work requirements in Nebraska and examines early data on outcomes for individuals subject to work requirements. Americans’ Challenges with Health Care Costs Sep 29, 2026 Issue Brief This data note reviews our recent polling data that finds that many Americans struggle to afford many aspects of health care, including disproportionate shares of uninsured adults, Black and Hispanic adults and those with lower incomes. according to oxygenation interface: a prospective cohort study 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月03日 来源:The Egyptian Journal of Critical Care Medicine 0.3 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Original article Open access 背景:清醒俯卧位(APP)已广泛用于COVID-19相关急性呼吸窘迫综合征(ARDS)患者,但其有效性可能因氧疗接口而异。本研究旨在比较不同氧疗接口下对APP的反应,并识别反应预测因素。 方法:研究人员于2021年3月至5月开展前瞻性观察性研究,纳入因重型至危重型COVID-19入住重症监护病房(ICU)的成年患者。在入ICU后24 h内,使用常规氧疗(COT)、高流量鼻氧(HFNO)和无创通气(NIV)实施至少30 min的APP,并在可耐受时按序应用。每次APP前和APP后20 min测量动脉血气。反应定义为PaO 2 /FiO 2 比值增加≥20%。 结果:共纳入56例患者。不同接口反应率不同:COT下25.5%,HFNO下34.4%,NIV下43.9%。COT和HFNO下反应者插管率较低(p=0.03和p=0.01),HFNO下反应者住院时间较短(p=0.018)。除NIV外(p=0.6),所有接口下非反应者死亡率较高。较高的体质量指数(BMI)与COT和HFNO下的反应相关,受试者工作特征(ROC)分析识别出预测切点在27.3至28.3 2 <90%),危重型COVID-19包括需要重症监护支持的ARDS、脓毒性休克或多器官衰竭患者。该区分重要,因为对APP等干预的生理反应可能随疾病严重度不同。既有研究支持APP改善自主呼吸呼吸衰竭患者氧合,包括因ARDS入住ICU者,但其降低插管率和死亡率的作用、耐受性及最佳持续时间仍不清楚。因此,本研究拟比较不同氧疗接口下APP反应,包括口插管需求、死亡和住院时间,并识别俯卧位反应预测因素。研究来源为TUNISIA的ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院。 研究人员开展什么研究、结论及意义 研究人员在ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院医疗ICU开展前瞻性观察性研究,纳入2021年3月至5月因COVID-19确诊重型至危重型(按WHO定义)入住、自主呼吸的成年患者。非纳入标准为患者拒绝俯卧位;排除标准为首次会话耐受差和/或临床情况严重恶化。研究人员收集人口学和临床数据,随访至出院,记录插管、插管时间和死亡。结论为:APP反应因氧疗接口不同;阳性反应可能与临床结局改善相关,尤其在常规氧疗(COT,通过鼻导管或面罩等常规给氧)和高流量鼻氧(HFNO,经鼻高流量氧疗)下;较高体质量指数(BMI,体重与身高平方之比)可能预测有利反应。意义在于提示APP应纳入阶梯式呼吸支持策略,HFNO可能在疗效与耐受之间较适合与APP联合,早期识别反应者可能有助于临床管理并避免延迟插管;但观察性设计、短时会话和接口序贯应用要求谨慎解释,需进一步随机研究证实。 关键技术方法 研究人员开展前瞻性观察性队列研究,队列来源为ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院医疗ICU,2021年3—5月因WHO定义重型至危重型COVID-19入住、自主呼吸的成年患者。纳入56例在入ICU 24 h内接受至少一次≥30 min APP者;COT、HFNO和无创通气(NIV,无需人工气道的正压通气)在可耐受时序贯应用。每次APP前后20 min在稳定氧合设置下行动脉血气,反应定义为动脉血氧分压/吸入氧分数比值(PaO 2 /FiO 2 )增加≥20%。收集插管、插管时间、死亡和住院时间。统计采用描述性分析、Student检验、卡方检验、趋势卡方检验、Kaplan-Meier与log-rank检验、受试者工作特征(ROC)曲线和曲线下面积(AUC)评估BMI预测价值,SPSS v23,P<0.05。 研究结果 入组与APP实施。研究期间117例因确诊SARS COV 2肺炎入住ICU,115例合格,56例接受至少一次>30 min APP。COT下51例,HFNO下32例,NIV下41例;COT反应率25.5%(n=13),HFNO 34.4%(n=11),NIV 43.9%(n=18)。全部患者至少在1种接口下接受俯卧位,32例为反应者;47例使用2种接口,其中8例为反应者;22例连续使用3种接口,其中2例为反应者。通过比较不同接口下APP前后PaO 2 /FiO 2 变化及反应率,研究人员得出反应因接口不同而异。 患者特征。多数为男性(n=41,72.5%),平均年龄55.9±15岁;在各接口下反应者与非反应者年龄多无差异,但1种接口反应者较非反应者年轻(52.13±15.8 vs 61±12.3,P=0.02)。平均BMI为28 kg/m2,在COT、HFNO、1种和2种接口反应者中更高(COT,p=0.01;HFNO,p=0.01;1种接口,p=0.03;2种接口,p=0.04)。高血压占24.6%(n=14),糖尿病占26.8%(n=15),各接口两组无差异。所有患者入院时均为ARDS,多为重度(45.1%)至中度(45.1%);胸部CT病变>75%者占15.2%,50%—75%者占50%,各接口两组无差异。入院PaO 2 在COT反应者中较低(66.9 vs 83.7,p=0.03)。平均耐受时间37 min,最大60 min,各组无差异。由此得出,高BMI和较低入院PaO 2 可能与某些接口下反应相关。 预后。插管率为42.9%(n=24),平均于入院后4天。COT非反应者机械通气需求显著更高(24[64.9] vs 4[30.8],p=0.03),1种接口组中非反应者也更高(反应者1[12.5] vs 非反应者24[61.5],p=0.01)。非反应者更多发生院内感染,尤其是呼吸机相关性肺炎(VAP)(HFNO非反应者50% vs 反应者9.1%,p=0.023;1种接口非反应者58% vs 反应者32%,p=0.04)。平均住院时间10±3天,HFNO反应者显著更短(9±3 vs 14±10天,p=0.018)。死亡率为46.4%(n=26),除NIV外(反应者38.9% vs 非反应者39%,p=0.6),所有接口非反应者死亡率更高。通过比较反应者与非反应者的插管、感染、住院时间和死亡,研究人员发现阳性反应在COT和HFNO下可能与较好临床结局相关。 BMI预测反应。由于COT、HFNO、1种和2种接口下反应者BMI显著更高,研究人员以ROC曲线寻找预测APP反应的BMI切点。结果BMI切点为27.3—28.3 kg/m2,AUC为0.68—0.82,敏感性为92.3%—65.6%,特异性为63.2%—71.4%。由此得出,较高BMI可能是某些接口下APP反应的预测因素。 讨论部分总结 讨论指出,在这一重症至危重型COVID-19 ICU患者前瞻性队列中,APP生理反应因氧疗接口不同:COT下较有限,HFNO下居中,NIV下较高。以APP后20 min PaO 2 /FiO 2 早期改善定义的阳性反应,在COT和HFNO下与较好临床结局相关,包括机械通气需求和死亡率,但在NIV下未显示。较高的BMI(切点27.3—28.3 kg/m2)可能是某些接口下反应的预测因素。研究人员分阶段从COT(无呼气末正压[PEEP])到HFNO(低PEEP)再到NIV(高PEEP)改变接口,并在入ICU 24 h内实施以减少疾病演变偏倚;短时30 min基于患者耐受和既往研究。反应定义20%与X.Elharrar等和Oliveira等一致,而文献中俯卧位反应定义异质。APP生理机制包括改善通气/灌注匹配、复张依赖肺区、减少肺内分流,这在COVID-19肺灌注失调和分流所致低氧中尤其相关。COT下APP似乎降低反应者死亡率,但未改善插管或住院时间;Padr?o等在急诊回顾队列中50例常规氧患者1—4 h俯卧位,50%患者SpO 2 /FiO 2 增加10%,APP对插管、无机械通气天数和死亡无益。接口差异具临床意义:COT无PEEP可能限制肺泡复张,HFNO提供低水平PEEP并减少解剖死腔,可能增强APP生理益处;这与Ehrmann等大型多中心meta试验显示APP显著减少HFNO患者插管需求一致,PROFLO随机临床试验也显示APP联合HFNO降低插管率和住院时间。尽管NIV反应率最高,但未转化为临床结局改善;这可能反映指征混杂,因NIV通常用于更严重呼吸衰竭患者,疾病严重度可能超过俯卧位益处;NIV俯卧位还可能患者-呼吸机不同步、面罩不耐受和呼吸功增加。高BMI与APP反应相关是本研究新发现,肥胖与功能残气量降低和仰卧位背侧肺压缩有关,俯卧位可能带来更大肺泡复张和氧合改善;近期meta分析提示超重和肥胖患者可能从俯卧位更多获益,但未定义具体预测阈值。研究优势为前瞻性比较不同接口下非插管清醒ICU患者APP反应。局限包括:接口序贯应用为非随机,是主要偏倚来源;反应定义为20 min短期氧合改善,可能不反映持续获益或长期结局;样本量较小,亚组分析可能降低统计效能并增加多重比较的I类错误风险;俯卧位平均37 min较短,可能限制获益;指南建议短时30 min至2 h每日重复,仍需更新包括APP启动资格、次数、每日平均时间、随访方案、并发症和失败早期识别及标准化插管标准。临床意义上,APP应整合入阶梯呼吸支持策略;鉴于疗效与耐受平衡,HFNO似乎最适合与APP联合;基于短期氧合改善和BMI早期识别反应者可能帮助临床医生调整管理并避免延迟插管;反之,无反应尤其在高阶支持如NIV下应促使重新评估并考虑有创机械通气。 研究结论翻译 短时间清醒俯卧位可行且安全。对清醒俯卧位的反应似乎因所用氧疗接口而异。阳性反应可能与结局改善相关,尤其是在常规氧疗和高流量鼻氧下。较高的BMI可能预测有利反应。由于观察性设计、俯卧时长较短和接口序贯应用,这些发现应谨慎解释。需要进一步随机研究证实这些结果。 h俯卧位,50%患者SpO/FiO增加10%,APP对插管、无机械通气天数和死亡无益。接口差异具临床意义:COT无PEEP可能限制肺泡复张,HFNO提供低水平PEEP并减少解剖死腔,可能增强APP生理益处;这与Ehrmann等大型多中心meta试验显示APP显著减少HFNO患者插管需求一致,PROFLO随机临床试验也显示APP联合HFNO降低插管率和住院时间。尽管NIV反应率最高,但未转化为临床结局改善;这可能反映指征混杂,因NIV通常用于更严重呼吸衰竭患者,疾病严重度可能超过俯卧位益处;NIV俯卧位还可能患者-呼吸机不同步、面罩不耐受和呼吸功增加。高BMI与APP反应相关是本研究新发现,肥胖与功能残气量降低和仰卧位背侧肺压缩有关,俯卧位可能带来更大肺泡复张和氧合改善;近期meta分析提示超重和肥胖患者可能从俯卧位更多获益,但未定义具体预测阈值。研究优势为前瞻性比较不同接口下非插管清醒ICU患者APP反应。局限包括:接口序贯应用为非随机,是主要偏倚来源;反应定义为20 min短期氧合改善,可能不反映持续获益或长期结局;样本量较小,亚组分析可能降低统计效能并增加多重比较的I类错误风险;俯卧位平均37 min较短,可能限制获益;指南建议短时30 min至2 h每日重复,仍需更新包括APP启动资格、次数、每日平均时间、随访方案、并发症和失败早期识别及标准化插管标准。临床意义上,APP应整合入阶梯呼吸支持策略;鉴于疗效与耐受平衡,HFNO似乎最适合与APP联合;基于短期氧合改善和BMI早期识别反应者可能帮助临床医生调整管理并避免延迟插管;反之,无反应尤其在高阶支持如NIV下应促使重新评估并考虑有创机械通气。研究结论翻译短时间清醒俯卧位可行且安全。对清醒俯卧位的反应似乎因所用氧疗接口而异。阳性反应可能与结局改善相关,尤其是在常规氧疗和高流量鼻氧下。较高的BMI可能预测有利反应。由于观察性设计、俯卧时长较短和接口序贯应用,这些发现应谨慎解释。需要进一步随机研究证实这些结果。 Politics Money Arts Justice Environment Newsletter Ways to support Gov. Jared Polis gets vaccinated to protect against flu and COVID-19 By John Daley · Oct. 1, 2026, 6:44 pm Share: Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Lauren Brown, a registered nurse and supervisor with the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment's Mobile Public Health Clinic, gives Gov. Jared Polis his annual flu and COVID vaccinations in his office at the Colorado State Capitol. Oct. 1, 2026. With flu numbers in Colorado starting to mount, Gov. Jared Polis got vaccinated in his office at the Capitol Thursday. He rolled up his sleeves (but not too far, he was wearing a short sleeved shirt) for two shots: one for flu and one for COVID-19. “Just trying to lead by example here and show other Coloradans how easy this is. You barely feel these things,” he said as he smiled for a photo. Nearly 7% of Coloradans have already gotten their flu shot, according to the state health department. That’s a decrease of more than 1% from this time last year. More than 6-thousand Coloradans were hospitalized with flu over the past year, according to the state’s viral respiratory disease dashboard. At Christmas last year, hospitals were jammed with a record number of flu patients who needed to be admitted — nearly 800 by New Year’s Eve. Polis said he gets the shots both for himself and other folks he spends time with. “My parents are in their 80s and I want to reduce the chance that I get something,” he said. “They've already gotten theirs, so I'm excited to reduce the chance that I'll be out of commission for a while or spread these to other people I know.” Vaccines for flu, updated COVID shots and RSV are available at pharmacies, clinics and doctors' offices. Last season, about a third of Coloradans got vaccinated for flu, which was a bit lower than the year before. Less than 14 percent of Colorado residents got a COVID-19 immunization, according to the state, which was lower than the year before. Doctors and major medical groups say getting vaccinated is the best way to avoid serious illness from these viruses. And it appears more flu cases are brewing in Colorado. “We have been seeing a flurry of activity much before we anticipated. We're starting to see flu cases much before that we typically see around November or December of each year,” said Dr. Edwin Asturias, a pediatric infectious disease physician at the Colorado School of Public Health. This is a good time, he said, for people to be ready for the flu season that comes as soon as the vaccine is already here. “I think we may have an earlier season than other years in the past,” said Asturias, a former member of the U.S. Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The state health department's viral respiratory dashboard showed 36 people are now hospitalized with flu, as of the end of September. A month ago there was only one. Additionally, 34 people were hospitalized with COVID. UCHealth infectious diseases expert Dr. Michelle Barron said her health system saw four times as many positive flu cases in September than the same month last year. “So, flu is already circulating,” she said. She said now is a good time to get your shots, just as the governor did Thursday. “Anyone over 6 months of age should get a flu and COVID shot. I would strongly recommend the very young and the very old,” she said. She defined that loosely as anyone over 65. She said pregnant women should also get their shots, because they're also very susceptible to flu and COVID. You care. You want to know what is really going on these days, especially in Colorado. We can help you keep up. The Lookout is a free, daily email newsletter with news and happenings from all over Colorado. Sign up here and we will see you in the morning! Contact Our Staff Purple Knight Small Business Guide Hub Communications All News Academics Planning for the future: St. Mike’s group explores what worked (and didn’t) during VT’s COVID-19 response by Rylee Anderson '27 October 2, 2026 Share From left, past Saint Michael's College research student Elsa Gordon poses with current researchers Emily Gates and Damascene Niyongere after presenting on their research through the SOCKS grant. (Courtesy of Candas Pinar) October 2, 2026 Rylee Anderson '27 Vermont is considered to have had one of the most successful responses to the COVID-19 pandemic in the U.S. when the virus brought the world to a standstill in 2020. A research group at St. Mike’s is asking why. Over the past four years, the multidisciplinary project has given students real-world research experience while allowing faculty to explore effective communication strategies in hopes of limiting the effects of future public health emergencies. This past summer, a group of undergraduates worked on the project alongside Sociology Professor Candas Pinar, Computer Science Professor Bradford Demarest, and Political Science and Public Health Professor Patricia Siplon. They are particularly interested in Gov. Phil Scott’s press conferences from that time, beginning in March 2020. They are analyzing Scott’s speeches and answers to reporters’ questions through multiple lenses, including public health. Vermont Gov. Phil Scott gives a press conference, which was streamed by ORCA Media, in March 2020 explaining the “Stay Home, Stay Safe” initiative to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Saint Michael’s College professors and students are currently several years into a five-year grant to study why Scott’s messaging was so effective in Vermont. The research is part of the University of Vermont’s broader Science of Online Corpora, Knowledge, and Stories (SOCKS) project, which is federally funded through Vermont EPSCoR (The Vermont Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research). While the analysis methods vary among the members of the Saint Michael’s team, they’re all focused on the same question: whether Scott’s language called on social capital and how that affected Vermonters’ actions during the pandemic. Social capital, at its core, is what holds communities together. Pinar explained that it is “the connections and bonds that exist between people. “It’s also what we have access to as a result of those bonds,” Pinar added. “We might get access to new information, or if you live in a community where people look out for each other, you might enjoy a higher level of security.” The team is looking through transcripts from videos of Phil Scott’s speeches to dial in on when and how he references this kind of ideology. Saint Michael’s College faculty and students discuss progress they’ve made so far on research into Vermont Gov. Phil Scott’s COVID-19 messaging and why it was so effective in the state. (Courtesy of Candas Pinar) Studying stories and social capital The SOCKS project, in essence, aims to study words and stories, and their power. These researchers are studying how Gov. Scott used stories and specific language during COVID-19 press conferences to bring communities together and encourage adherence to health guidelines. The project began with Pinar and Siplon partnering with former Saint Michael’s Criminology Professor Krista Billingsley, who served as the project’s Primary Investigator (PI). Demarest later joined the group, and Pinar took over as the PI after Billingsley pursued new opportunities beyond the College. “We were really interested in Vermont’s response to the COVID- 19 pandemic, because it was such a leader in this country,” Pinar said. “We knew that Vermont is known for being a state that has a very coherent sense of community, and very high levels of what we call social capital. So, we brought those two interests together into this project where we were wondering, to what extent did political leaders in Vermont during the pandemic really highlight those stories of community in their communications with the public?” Social capital is a major topic in the social sciences, specifically sociology, but to others, it’s an elusive term. When she first joined the SOCKS team, Health Science major Clara Hershey ’28 was unfamiliar with the concept. “I’ve never taken a sociology class,” Hershey said. Social capital, she added, was “the bulk of what our research team was focused on. I did a lot of reading the literature and trying to grasp what social capital was.” From left, past Saint Michael’s College research student Elsa Gordon poses with current researchers Emily Gates and Damascene Niyongere after presenting on their research through the SOCKS project. (Courtesy of Candas Pinar) The grant began at the tail end of the pandemic, and Pinar said that “it was the forefront of a lot of what we were doing as public health professors.” The research continued this summer, with six students involved. Emily Gates ’27 has been working with Pinar for the past two summers, while Lavender Gaudette ’27 and Hershey joined the team this year. Maya Clough ’28, who is also working on research with Chemistry Professor Megan Browning, has helped collect data for the team by transcribing the press conference videos into text that they could analyze. “All of the data that we’re working with has to be created,” Pinar said. “That requires a very elaborate and tedious process that Maya has spearheaded this summer. The original data set was created by another undergrad, but because of Maya’s contributions, we now have language from press conferences before the COVID-19 pandemic so that we can compare over time.” Comparing press conference language before and during the pandemic is just one way the project is constantly growing and evolving. The team is also analyzing Scott’s speeches against those of Chris Sununu, New Hampshire’s governor during the pandemic. Using computational linguistics to dig deeper Technology is playing an important role in this research, with Computer Science Professor Demarest bringing his expertise into the equation. “My focus is on computational linguistics, those tools that are more quantitative,” Demarest said. “Like trying to get a general description of a great pile of text so people can do things like noticing just where he’s talking about Vermonters instead of having to go through with a fine-tooth comb.” Saint Michael’s Professors Trish Siplon (Political Science and Public Health), Candas Pinar (Sociology), and Bradford Demarest (Computer Science) pose for a photo together at the New England Political Science Association’s conference. (Photo courtesy of Candas Pinar) Samantha Galle ’29 worked under Demarest’s mentorship this summer, and, like Demarest, comes from a background in linguistics. “I’m learning the more technical side of it,” Galle said. “I feel like you can’t fully understand how something works, even if you’re zeroed in on a particular subject like we are, unless you look at it from multiple different angles that seem to have no correlation.” Learning tools like Python and using the SOCKS “Hedonometer” instrument, which measures the happiness of large populations over time by analyzing social media data, Demarest and Galle have been diving deeper into the language Scott used in his speeches. The tools help them determine whether words are “good” or “bad,” “happy” or “unhappy,” and how they relate to other words. “We found there’s a strong correlation between ‘goodness’ and ‘power,’ as well as a strong negative correlation between ‘goodness’ and ‘danger,’” Galle said. “We gathered all this data, but we can’t really make sense of it just yet until we compare it to a control, which will be transcripts from a non-COVID-era press conference that Phil Scott has done.” The research continues into the school year, as the grant covers a five-year period. Looking at where Vermont was lacking Political Science and Public Health Professor Siplon is probing another question in this same vein with the help of Damascene Niyongere ’27, another student who has been part of this project for two summers. They are looking at where Vermont and Scott didn’t do as well, namely the impact of COVID-19 on the incarceration system. “What we’re looking at is how Vermont did or didn’t use the same social capital approach with regard to its incarceration system,” Siplon said. Like many other states, Vermont had to come up with sets of policies and ways of dealing with people who were incarcerated during the pandemic. The incarceration system was one of the highest-risk areas in the state since, like nursing homes, it housed groups of at-risk people in close quarters. “Vermont doesn’t have the capacity to house all of its incarcerated people in the state, so it essentially outsourced people, and their experience was pretty bad,” Siplon said, alluding to the state’s longtime practice of sending incarcerated people to prisons outside Vermont. “We’re looking at both the policies themselves and how those policies were, and sometimes weren’t, talked about.” Damascene Niyongere ’27 speaks at the annual summer research kickoff brunch at Saint Michael’s in summer 2026, describing the work he’s doing through the SOCKS project with Political Science and Public Health Professor Trish Siplon. (Photo by Christina Cummings ’25) Niyongere and Siplon reviewed reports from the Vermont Department of Corrections, public health literature, state policies, and news coverage to discover the impact of COVID-19 on Vermont’s six correctional facilities. Incarcerated individuals were placed in quarantine when exposed to the virus, and the group sought to find out how this affected the people in the facilities. “While quarantine was an important control measure, our research found that prolonged isolation contributed to increased anxiety, depression, loneliness, and worsened mental health,” Niyongere said. The research also found higher transmission rates in state correctional facilities, with nearly 70% of those tested in 2020 being found positive for the virus. “This research showed that Vermont failed to uphold the same level of concern for social capital of incarcerated people that they showed in the general population,” Niyongere explained. A ‘multi-year, multi-disciplinary, multi-level’ project This research has been a long and winding journey, but at its core, it reflects the values of Saint Michael’s College, particularly the close student-professor collaboration that occurs on campus. “That’s why I’m at a place like Saint Michael’s,” Pinar said. “I love the fact that I can work on this project and have people just to check in with. It’s so much more fun and positive, and I think it produces better science, honestly.” The students, like the faculty working on the project, each bring a unique perspective to the table. From Gates, a Digital Media & Marketing and Sociology/Anthropology double major, to Hershey, a Health Sciences major, the students are branching out beyond their academic disciplines to experience real-world research with myriad applications. “Being on a research team, I’ve been able to see and experience the process of troubleshooting and backtracking,” Hershey said. “It’s really my first experience doing research like this, and I’ve been able to understand how do you pivot in a different direction? How do you look at something differently?” Like any research group, the team faced challenges. Galle, who came from a linguistics background, had to learn new computer science tools before using them for the project, which made for less efficient results. Pinar’s team, including Gates, Hershey, and Gaudette, had to decide whether to double down on explicit social capital references or include inferred references. They also moved away from using the CDC’s Tool for Thematic Analysis and found new tools that worked best for their research. However, despite these challenges, the group still gained valuable research experience and is working toward finishing the final two years of the research grant. They hope their research will provide valuable information about governments’ emergency responses. “If and when there’s another pandemic, we can take what we learned about effective communication strategies that help to build common ground among people,” Pinar said. “But the work extends beyond pandemics. You can think about any emergency situation.” For example, Pinar said more climate-related human-generated disasters are likely scenarios that societies will need to face in the future. “Learning as much as we can about communication strategies that can create an effective, collective response is really important,” she said. Students had the opportunity to present their research at the University of Vermont last spring, and they hope to present at another conference in New Hampshire in October. “We have our own little community in its fourth year, and we have great student researchers, and also alumni who have come out of the program interested in what’s going on and in taking their skills into other places,” Siplon said. “This is my 29th year at St. Mike’s, and this is the first time that I’ve been in a multi-year, multi-disciplinary, multi-level project like this. It feels really special for me.” For all press inquiries contact Elizabeth Murray, Associate Director of Communications at Saint Michael's College. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Business Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Your guide to vaccines for flu, COVID-19 and RSV in Wisconsin Madeline Heim Milwaukee Journal Sentinel Oct. 1, 2026, 5:05 a.m. CT The Wisconsin Department of Health Services released annual recommendations for flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines for this fall. Flu and COVID-19 vaccines are recommended for residents 6 months and older, especially those most at risk of severe illness. One dose of the RSV is recommended for all adults 75 and older, some 50 and older and during 32-36 weeks of pregnancy. Local physicians say they are glad to field questions from their patients about which vaccines to take and when. It's officially fall – leaves are turning, evening sunlight is fading, and respiratory viruses will soon start circulating at higher levels. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Sept. 30 released its annual recommendations for vaccines to protect against the flu and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, as well as updated COVID-19 shots. The recommendations lean on guidance from major medical organizations, not the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose immunization committee is currently inactive due to federal turmoil around vaccines and is not expected to issue updated guidelines. Across Wisconsin, about 11,000 people were hospitalized during last year's respiratory season with the flu, COVID-19 or RSV, chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases Dr. Ryan Westergaard said in a Sept. 30 news briefing. "That's something that you wouldn't wish on anyone," he said. Dr. Bill Calawerts, a family medicine physician and assistant professor at the Medical College of Wisconsin, said he welcomes discussions about which vaccines are appropriate and when. "I and my physician colleagues are not offended by questions," Calawerts said. "If you really want to talk about it, don't be ashamed to bring questions to your clinician." Vaccines for respiratory viruses are covered by most insurance plans and are available at doctors' offices, local health departments, pharmacies and pop-up vaccine clinics. Those who need help paying for vaccines can use the Vaccines for Children and Vaccines for Adults programs. Here's what you need to know about the shots available in Wisconsin this fall. Updated COVID-19 vaccine The state health department recommends that all residents ages 6 months and older receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine. These vaccines are being updated yearly to target the latest strains of the virus. The vaccine is especially recommended for adults 65 and older, as well as others who are more likely to become seriously ill from contracting COVID-19. COVID-19 vaccines are most effective for the first three months after receiving the shot, offering protection against serious illness. Last year, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. retracted the recommendation for healthy children and pregnant people to receive the COVID-19 vaccine, a move that has since been temporarily blocked by a federal judge. Such changes caused people to be unsure of whether their insurer would cover the shot. Wisconsin health officials issued guidance still broadly supporting the vaccine, but not many people got it. Less than 14% of residents got an updated COVID-19 vaccine during the 2025-26 respiratory virus season, immunization data show. Seniors were the most likely to receive it, with more than one in three people 65 and older getting the updated shot. This year, federal health officials delayed COVID-19 vaccine doses available through the Vaccines for Children program, which offers free vaccines to the uninsured or underinsured. Wisconsin's allocation was delayed, Westergaard confirmed, but eventually arrived, and Vaccines for Children providers were able to start ordering doses Sept. 28. Orders for about 5,000 doses have been filled already, he said. Calawerts said he is still recommending the COVID-19 vaccine to most of his patients. "I describe it like wearing a helmet when you're riding a bike. That's only really your personal choice, how much risk you're willing to take, and ultimately it's totally your decision to make as well," Calawerts said. "It's an extra layer of protection if you get an infection." COVID-19 activity in Wisconsin is currently very low, according to state respiratory virus data. Flu vaccine State health officials recommend everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine, especially older adults, people with chronic conditions, young children and pregnant people. Already, the state is seeing a slight increase in influenza cases, Westergaard said. The flu is difficult for scientists to prepare for, and each year, they try to predict what type of vaccine will offer the most protection against it. That means it's not always a perfect match. Last year, for example, the shot didn't protect as well against a new strain of the virus that emerged. Calawerts said he's up front with his patients about that, but still points out that the flu vaccine is meant to lower risk of severe complications. Studies have shown the flu vaccine can significantly reduce people's risk of severe outcomes if they contract the disease. This year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a new type of flu vaccine called mFLUSIVA for use in people 50 and older. It's the first flu vaccine to use mRNA technology, similar to some COVID-19 vaccines. In clinical trials, the vaccine was about 27% more effective at preventing influenza than a traditional flu vaccine. The mRNA flu vaccine will be available in Wisconsin, Westergaard said, but only through private providers, and it may not be covered by all insurance plans for people 50 to 64. "It's a newer tool in our toolkit, so this season might be one where uptake is lower than others," he said. "The data appear to be very favorable in terms of effectiveness and safety so far." The number of Wisconsin residents getting the flu vaccine has been falling since the pandemic. Last season, about one in three residents of all ages received it. Experts say it is safe to receive the flu vaccine and COVID-19 vaccine at the same time. They recommend getting the flu shot by the end of October. RSV vaccine Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, causes cold-like symptoms and is usually mild in adults and older healthy children. In infants, older adults and people with heart or lung diseases, it can be more serious. The state health department recommends a one-time dose of the RSV for people over 50 who are at increased risk of severe disease, for all adults 75 and older, and during 32-36 weeks of pregnancy between Sept. 1 and March 1. If the RSV vaccine isn't given during pregnancy, health officials recommend an RSV antibody shot for infants younger than 8 months. The RSV vaccine can be given at the same time as other vaccines. As of Sept. 23, nearly 19% of Wisconsin residents 50 and older have received an RSV vaccine, according to state immunization data, and about 36% of residents 75 and older. Last respiratory virus season, close to 26,800 doses of antibody to protect against RSV were administered to Wisconsin infants, the state health department said. RSV activity in Wisconsin is currently very low. Madeline Heim covers health and the environment for the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. Contact her at 920-996-7266 or mheim@usatodayco.com. supplementary_news.content_title: Magnetic Stimulation Improves Long COVID “Brain Fog”
supplementary_news.content: The therapy proved safe, well tolerated, and easily administered by patients remotely at home. Credit: Neuroscience News Magnetic Stimulation Improves Long COVID “Brain Fog” FeaturedNeurologyNeuroscience ·September 30, 2026 Summary: A pilot clinical trial led by the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai shows that an at-home, non-invasive magnetic headset significantly improves cognitive performance and emotional well-being in adults suffering from long COVID “brain fog.” Published in Brain Communications, the triple-blind, sham-controlled study found that twice-weekly sessions of Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT) enhanced working memory, processing speed, and verbal learning, with therapeutic benefits persisting a full month after treatment ended. Key Facts: Targeted Brain Stimulation: Participants self-administered 15-minute sessions twice weekly for four weeks using an investigational headset delivering nonthermal radio-frequency low-amplitude magnetic fields (MMT) to the whole brain. Measurable Cognitive & Mood Gains: Active treatment produced significant gains in working memory, processing speed, verbal learning, and self-reported emotional well-being compared to an identical sham device. Durable Aftereffects: Cognitive improvements continued between the end of the four-week treatment window and the eight-week follow-up assessment, indicating lasting neuroplastic or anti-inflammatory changes. Source: Mount Sinai Health System Among the constellation of symptoms defining post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), commonly termed long COVID, cognitive dysfunction remains among the most debilitating. Millions of individuals describe a persistent “brain fog” characterized by slowed processing speed, executive dysfunction, working memory lapses, and attention deficits that derail employment and daily life. Emerging neuropathological evidence indicates that long COVID cognitive deficits stem from a combination of sustained neuroinflammation, microvascular endotheliopathy, and mitochondrial metabolic exhaustion within neural tissue. Yet, despite the vast global disease burden, clinically validated therapeutic interventions remain exceedingly rare. In a randomized, triple-blind pilot trial published in Brain Communications, investigators from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai evaluated whether biophysical neuromodulation could counter these entrenched post-viral neurological symptoms. The researchers tested Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT), a proprietary, non-invasive technology developed by clinical-stage biophysics company Fareon® that delivers low-amplitude, nonthermal radio-frequency magnetic fields across the cortex. “Cognitive symptoms are among the most persistent and disabling manifestations of long COVID, yet evidence-based treatment options have been sparse,” said co-senior author Jacqueline Becker, Ph.D., clinical neuropsychologist and assistant professor of medicine at Icahn Mount Sinai. “What is particularly encouraging about these findings is that we observed improvements across several cognitive domains, as well as in daily functioning and well-being, and that these improvements persisted even after treatment ended.” Triple-Blind, At-Home Intervention The clinical trial enrolled 30 adults with objectively documented post-COVID cognitive impairment. Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive either active MMT or an indistinguishable sham treatment that looked, sounded, and operated identically. Subjects wore the headset at home for 15 minutes twice a week over a four-week period, monitored remotely by Mount Sinai clinical trial coordinators. The investigators assessed cognitive performance, mood, and quality-of-life metrics at baseline, at week four (conclusion of the intervention), and at week eight (four-week post-treatment follow-up). The home-administered protocol proved safe, feasible, and well tolerated, with participants exceeding the 80% protocol completion threshold without significant device-related adverse events. Patients receiving active MMT demonstrated marked improvements in objective neuropsychological endpoints, including: Working Memory: Enhanced capacity to retain and manipulate information over short intervals. Processing Speed: Increased cognitive reaction time and task execution speed. Verbal Learning: Stronger retention and recall during verbal memory tasks. Emotional Well-Being: Reductions in mood disturbance and gains in self-reported daily quality of life. Lasting Neuroplastic Improvements Beyond Treatment Critically, the therapeutic gains did not diminish when patients took off the headset at the end of week four. During the subsequent four-week washout observation period, participants in the active cohort exhibited continued cognitive and mood improvements through week eight. While the primary mechanisms remain under investigation, preclinical models of MMT indicate that low-amplitude magnetic oscillations can suppress chronic neuroinflammation, downregulate reactive microglial activation, and support mitochondrial bioenergetics, biological pathways known to be compromised in post-viral encephalopathies. “According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, roughly 7 percent of Americans are experiencing symptoms related to long COVID, and a majority of these people report cognitive symptoms as amongst their most troubling and disabling symptoms,” said co-senior author David Putrino, Ph.D., Nash Family Director of the Cohen Center for Recovery From Complex Chronic Illness at Icahn Mount Sinai. “There is an urgent need to find answers and effective treatments for the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who are struggling with long COVID. This first-in-human study is a promising start for a completely novel therapy that is showing great potential.” The researchers emphasize that while these initial pilot results are promising, MMT remains an investigational therapy that requires verification in larger multicenter cohorts to determine optimal dosage schedules, long-term durability, and the exact biological mechanisms restoring network function. DOI: 10.1093/braincomms/fcag364 Abstract Microtesla magnetic therapy for cognitive impairment in long COVID: a randomized pilot study Cognitive impairment is common in post-acute sequelae of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 infection (long COVID) and substantially affects function and quality of life. Evidence suggests that sustained neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular dysfunction, and mitochondrial impairment contribute to cognitive symptoms. Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT) is a transcranial, low-amplitude radiofrequency magnetic field intervention that has shown anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in preclinical models, suggesting potential value in long COVID and other neurological disorders. COVID-19 was associated with increased risks of all six allergic conditions in the full cohort. Findings highlighted the potential value of monitoring for allergic disease after COVID-19. COVID-19 infection was associated with an increased risk of six newly diagnosed allergic conditions in a retrospective cohort study of children and adults aged 1–64 years. The findings highlighted a potential allergic disease burden following infection, with different patterns observed in children and active-duty service members. Assessing Allergic Disease After COVID-19 Researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study using 1:2 propensity score matching to evaluate the association between COVID-19 exposure and the development of allergic conditions over 18 months. The outcomes were atopic dermatitis, asthma, food allergy, rhinoconjunctivitis, medication allergy, and urticaria. The analysis focused on incident conditions, examining new diagnoses during follow-up. Researchers calculated hazard ratios for each outcome across the full cohort and conducted separate analyses in children and active-duty service members. These subgroup analyses examined whether the associations observed across the study population were also present in these groups. Associations Differ Between Population Groups In the full cohort, COVID-19 infection was associated with significantly increased hazard ratios for all six allergic conditions. The findings therefore extended across respiratory, skin, food, and medication-related outcomes rather than being confined to a single diagnosis. Among active-duty service members, statistically significant associations were observed for asthma and rhinoconjunctivitis. In children, infection was significantly associated with five of the six conditions, with food allergy being the exception. Higher sponsor rank, assessed as a potential surrogate for socioeconomic status, was associated with a slightly lower risk of developing asthma. This association provided an additional finding concerning socioeconomic circumstances, although sponsor rank represented a proxy measure. Clinical Implications of Allergic Disease Risk The findings added to evidence of an association between COVID-19 infection and subsequent allergic disease in both children and adults. The authors emphasised the potential public health burden and the importance of monitoring for allergic conditions after infection to support prompt intervention. They also suggested a possible mechanistic link between COVID-19 and type two inflammation. However, the retrospective observational design means that the reported associations do not establish causation or confirm the proposed inflammatory mechanism. Reference: Clarion J et al. Post–COVID-19 onset of allergic conditions in a propensity-matched cohort of children and adults. Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol. 2026;137(2):185–193.e2. supplementary_news.content: Wednesday, September 30, 2026 Your care team can help you decide which vaccines to get and when. Flu, RSV, and COVID-19 are common illnesses caused by viruses. They tend to spread more in the fall and winter. Getting vaccinated lowers your risk of getting sick. If you do get sick, being vaccinated also lowers your risk of serious illness. Cancer and cancer treatment can weaken your immune system, which is your body’s defense against infection. This is called being immunocompromised. When your immune system is weakened, it’s harder for your body to fight off these viruses, and they’re more likely to make you very sick. Learn more about each vaccine Our experts answer common questions about each one. What to know about the flu Five myths about the flu shot RSV vaccines: Who can get one, side effects, and getting one at MSK COVID-19 vaccines for people with cancer or a weakened immune system Back to top Which vaccines should I get? It depends on your age, health, and treatment. Talk with your care team. They’ll tell you which vaccines to get and the best time to get them. Back to top Where can I get my vaccines? You can get them at MSK. Just ask your care team. You can also get them at most pharmacies. Back to top Should the people I live with get vaccinated too? Yes. When the people in your home and close circle get vaccinated, it helps protect both you and them. Encourage your family, caregivers, and close friends to stay up to date on their vaccines. supplementary_news.content_title: COVID-19 Drops Out Of World’s Top 10 Causes Of Death For First Time Since Pandemic Began - Health Policy Watch
supplementary_news.content: COVID dropped out of the 10 leading causes of deaths, while noncommunicable diseases caused 74% of deaths worldwide in 2023. COVID-19 dropped out of the world’s 10 leading causes of death in 2023 for the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, and only two years after it topped the list, according to new World Health Organization estimates released Friday. The virus directly killed an estimated 0.9 million people in 2023, ranking 14th, as global life expectancy climbed back to near its pre-pandemic level. WHO declared an end to COVID-19 as a global health emergency in May that year. Revised figures now rank COVID-19 as the world’s leading cause of death in 2021, with 9.4 million direct deaths. WHO’s earlier estimates had placed it second that year. Together with 5.3 million deaths in 2020, the new figures put the virus’s direct toll in the first two years of the pandemic at 14.7 million. Figures WHO published in 2024, based on an earlier round of estimates, showed the pandemic had cut global life expectancy by 1.8 years to 71.4 years between 2019 and 2021, back to 2012 levels. By 2023, global life expectancy at birth had recovered to 73.3 years, against 73.4 years in 2019. Healthy life expectancy, which counts only years lived in full health, rose to 62.8 years but remained 0.4 years below its 2019 level, when COVID-19 first struck. The estimates, which track more than 160 diseases and injuries from 2000 to 2023, show “a global health landscape that is both recovering from the pandemic and continuing to evolve,” WHO said. “Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Dr Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI. “The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health, while health systems are equipped to respond to the changing needs of populations.” Chronic diseases claim three in four lives; heart disease is still the top killer Eight of the 10 leading causes of death were noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), led by ischaemic heart disease, stroke and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). NCDs, which also include cancers, diabetes and dementia, accounted for 74% of deaths in 2023, up from 58% in 2000. For the first time, communicable diseases caused fewer than half of all deaths in low-income countries, which WHO called another step in the global epidemiological transition. Ischaemic heart disease killed about 9.5 million people in 2023, or 16% of the 61 million deaths worldwide, according to a WHO fact sheet published alongside the estimates. Deaths from the disease have risen by 3.0 million since 2000, the largest increase of any cause. Stroke killed 6.8 million people and COPD 3.6 million. Lower respiratory infections ranked fourth with 2.7 million deaths, back at their 2019 level and once again the deadliest communicable disease. Alzheimer disease and other dementias were the fifth leading cause of death, killing 2.1 million people. The conditions ranked 19th in 2000, and deaths have tripled since. Women accounted for 66% of dementia deaths. Deaths from HIV and AIDS fell 62% over the period, pushing the disease from seventh to 22nd. Diabetes, cancer and mental health conditions on the rise Diabetes deaths more than doubled to 2.0 million, while lung cancer deaths climbed from 1.1 million to 1.8 million. Kidney diseases rose from 17th to ninth, with deaths up 86%. Individual risk of ischaemic heart disease increased in WHO’s Western Pacific and South-East Asia regions even as the burden fell in much of the world. The risk of dying from diabetes also rose substantially, particularly in South-East Asia. The age-standardized rate of healthy life lost to depressive disorders rose by about 20% worldwide between 2019 and 2023, and by nearly 45% for anxiety disorders. WHO said mental health conditions and drug use disorders, alongside diabetes and dementia, were “contributing to a growing and changing burden of disease.” “The value of these estimates is not only in the numbers themselves,” Labrique said. “By showing how causes of death and disease burden are changing over time and across populations, they give countries evidence to help shape health policies and priorities.” Chronic diseases climb in low- and middle-income countries In low-income countries, seven of the 10 leading causes of death in 2023 were still communicable diseases. Lower respiratory infections have been the top killer there since around 2010, except in 2021, with more than 350,000 deaths every year since 2000 and no notable downward trend. Malaria, tuberculosis and HIV remained in the low-income top 10, though deaths from all three fell significantly. HIV deaths dropped 62%, and diarrhoeal disease deaths roughly halved, sliding from first to fifth. COPD, which ranks in the top 10 in every other income group, did not make the list. Lower-middle-income countries had a more even mix, with five NCDs, four communicable, maternal, neonatal or nutritional conditions and road injuries among their top 10. Deaths from ischaemic heart disease, stroke and COPD roughly doubled to take the top three places. Diabetes deaths more than tripled, lifting it from 15th to fifth, while HIV fell from sixth to 20th as deaths dropped about 70%. Upper-middle-income countries recorded the largest absolute rise in heart disease deaths of any group, nearly 1.8 million. Lung cancer deaths there more than doubled, an increase of 520,000 that is more than three times the combined rise in the other three income groups. It is also the only group where COVID-19 remained in the top 10, ranked 10th, though deaths have fallen 85% since the 2021 peak. Heart disease deaths fall in rich countries as dementia climbs High-income countries were the only group where deaths from ischaemic heart disease, stroke and stomach cancer fell, by 18%, 26% and 27% respectively. The two cardiovascular conditions still killed a combined 3.4 million people in 2023. Dementia deaths in high-income countries nearly quadrupled, lifting the conditions from seventh to third and past lung cancer. Hypertensive heart disease deaths more than doubled, rising from 15th to eighth. WHO attributed rising deaths from most leading causes in rich countries primarily to population ageing. “Understanding why people die is essential to improving how people live,” WHO said, while cautioning that accurate mortality data remain hard to collect in many low-income countries, where recording systems are often fragmented, incomplete or inconsistent. “When these data are disaggregated by factors such as age, sex and geographic location, they can reveal important inequalities and help identify where interventions are most urgently needed,” WHO said. supplementary_news.content_title: Post-COVID Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction: A Focus on Persistent Diarrhea
supplementary_news.content: Abstract Persistent gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection include diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, constipation, nausea, and other disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs), but these entities should not be treated as interchangeable. In a meta-analysis of long-COVID studies, any GI symptom was reported in approximately 22% of patients and diarrhea in 10%, although heterogeneity was very high. In a large US Veterans Affairs cohort, post-acute COVID-19 was associated with incident diarrhea (hazard ratio {HR}: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.52-1.65; excess burden 7.99 per 1,000 persons at one year) and irritable bowel syndrome (HR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.28-1.86). Prospective Rome IV cohorts report lower absolute rates of formally diagnosed DGBIs; one study found persistent DGBI symptoms in 6.6% at six months, with functional diarrhea in 2.2% and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in 2.5% at three months. Mechanistic evidence supports intestinal involvement during acute infection and demonstrates associations with epithelial/angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) perturbation, immune activation, barrier dysfunction, altered microbial taxa, and impaired microbial metabolite production. However, persistent viral RNA or antigen, dysbiosis, and gut-lung signaling remain proposed or associative mechanisms rather than established causes of chronic diarrhea. Treatment evidence specific to post-COVID functional diarrhea is sparse. A large synbiotic trial improved a broad “gastrointestinal upset” domain in post-acute COVID syndrome, but did not enroll a defined chronic diarrhea or Rome-positive population; probiotic and fecal microbiota transplantation trials showing GI effects were largely conducted during acute COVID-19. Therefore, current care should first exclude organic and medication-related causes, then apply phenotype-based management extrapolated from established diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) and functional-diarrhea practice while clearly acknowledging the limited post-COVID-specific evidence. Standardized definitions, pre-infection GI data, appropriate controls, functional microbiome measures, and dedicated randomized trials are priorities for future research. Introduction & Background Post-acute gastrointestinal manifestations of SARS-CoV-2 infection span a broad spectrum. Patients may report persistent or new diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, altered appetite, dyspepsia, reflux, constipation, or other bowel symptoms after the acute infection [1-4]. These symptom reports are clinically important, but they are not synonymous with a functional bowel disorder or disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). A DGBI is a positive clinical diagnosis based on a characteristic symptom pattern and accepted criteria after reasonable consideration of alternative organic disease; a symptom such as post-COVID diarrhea is initially a descriptive phenotype, not a diagnosis [5,6]. Acute GI involvement provides biologic plausibility for later bowel dysfunction. Diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, and anorexia were documented in early hospitalized and ambulatory cohorts, and viral RNA was detectable in stool in a substantial subset of patients [7-12]. Acute findings, however, should not be automatically extrapolated to chronic post-COVID symptoms because the relevant populations, time points, treatments, and competing causes differ. This review focuses on persistent or new-onset diarrhea after COVID-19 while placing it within the wider post-COVID GI spectrum. Diarrhea is emphasized because it is common enough to generate a measurable post-acute burden, overlaps clinically with functional diarrhea and diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D), and has direct implications for hydration, diagnostic evaluation, work capacity, and quality of life [1,3,4]. The review distinguishes broad post-COVID GI symptoms from Rome-defined DGBIs, separates acute from post-acute mechanistic and therapeutic evidence, and identifies where current management is based on post-COVID trials versus extrapolation from established gastroenterology practice. Review Methods of the narrative review This manuscript is a narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. For the peer-review revision, a targeted literature update was performed on September 19, 2026, using PubMed/MEDLINE for English-language publications from January 1, 2020, through September 19, 2026. The following two complementary search concepts were used: (1) (COVID-19 OR SARS-CoV-2) AND (long COVID OR post-COVID OR post-acute COVID-19 OR post-acute sequelae) AND (gastrointestinal OR diarrhea OR diarrhoea OR irritable bowel syndrome OR functional diarrhea OR disorders of gut-brain interaction OR microbiome OR dysbiosis); and (2) (COVID-19 OR SARS-CoV-2) AND (gastrointestinal OR diarrhea OR diarrhoea) AND (angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 {ACE2} OR permeability OR cytokine OR microbiome OR metabolite OR probiotic OR synbiotic OR fecal microbiota transplantation). We hand-checked reference lists of key systematic reviews, major cohort studies, randomized trials, and clinical guidelines for additional relevant publications. Eligible evidence included adult human observational studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews/meta-analyses, and major clinical guidance relevant to epidemiology, mechanisms, diagnosis, or treatment. Pediatric-only studies, animal-only studies, non-peer-reviewed preprints, isolated case reports, and studies without a relevant GI or post-infectious outcome were not prioritized. Acute-COVID studies were retained only when they directly informed GI mechanisms or intervention safety/efficacy and were explicitly identified as acute evidence. Duplicate publications were reconciled manually. Screening and synthesis were conducted at the narrative-review level; no independent dual-reviewer screening, formal risk-of-bias instrument, PRISMA flow diagram, or original quantitative pooling was performed. Effect estimates from the strongest studies are reported where available, and the limitations of this approach are addressed below. Terminology and scope For clarity, this review uses “post-COVID GI symptoms” as an umbrella description for GI complaints occurring after acute infection. “Post-COVID diarrhea” refers descriptively to persistent, recurrent, or new loose/watery stools after COVID-19 and does not imply a functional etiology. “Functional diarrhea” and “IBS-D” are Rome-defined DGBIs; IBS-D requires recurrent abdominal pain as a central feature, whereas functional diarrhea is characterized by loose/watery stools without predominant abdominal pain. “Post-infectious IBS” (PI-IBS) describes IBS that begins after an acute infectious illness in a person without pre-existing IBS. COVID-19 may act as an infectious trigger for PI-IBS, but a distinct “post-COVID IBS” mechanism has not been established [5,6,13,14]. Table 1 summarizes these operational distinctions among diarrhea-related post-COVID phenotypes. Epidemiology of post-COVID GI symptoms and DGBIs Quantitative Estimates The magnitude of post-COVID GI burden depends strongly on outcome definition. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of long COVID, the pooled frequency of any GI symptom was 22% (95% CI: 10%-41%); diarrhea was 10% (95% CI: 4%-23%), dyspepsia 20% (95% CI: 6%-50%), and IBS 17% (95% CI: 6%-37%). The very high heterogeneity (I2 approximately 96%-98% for several outcomes) limits use of these pooled percentages as patient-level predictions [3]. Large administrative cohorts quantify relative risk but may not establish a Rome-defined functional disorder. In the US Veterans Affairs study of 154,068 COVID-19 survivors, compared with contemporary controls, diarrhea had an HR of 1.58 (95% CI: 1.52-1.65) and an estimated excess one-year burden of 7.99 per 1,000 persons; IBS had an HR of 1.54 (95% CI: 1.28-1.86), and functional dyspepsia an HR of 1.36 (95% CI: 1.22-1.51) [1]. In a Bronx health-system cohort followed up to 3.5 years, 6.34% of 35,102 COVID-19 patients developed a new GI diagnosis versus 5.70% of controls; the adjusted HR for the composite GI outcome was 1.18 (95% CI: 1.12-1.25) [2]. These datasets demonstrate excess post-acute GI healthcare diagnoses but include outcomes broader than functional bowel disease. Prospective studies applying Rome IV criteria generally report lower absolute rates. Golla et al. followed 320 COVID-19 cases, 320 household controls, and 280 seronegative controls: 11.3% of cases reported new functional gastrointestinal disorder (FGID)/DGBI symptoms at one month, 8.4% at three months, and 6.6% at six months; at three months, IBS occurred in 2.5% and functional diarrhea in 2.2%, while no healthy controls developed FGID through six months [4]. In a separate case-control study, 5.3% of 280 COVID-19 patients met IBS criteria at six months, compared with one of 264 controls [15]. A 2024 meta-analysis estimated pooled post-COVID IBS incidence at 12%, but the pooled RR versus non-COVID controls was 1.23 (95% CI: 0.50-3.01), illustrating uncertainty generated by heterogeneous definitions, follow-up, and study design [16]. A 2025 multicenter analysis identified post-COVID DGBIs in 27 of 599 eligible patients (4.5%), again emphasizing that formally defined DGBIs represent a narrower group than all post-COVID GI symptoms [17]. Table 2 summarizes representative epidemiological studies and their quantitative findings. Diarrhea Versus Other GI Outcomes and Symptom Duration Diarrhea is a reproducible acute and post-acute symptom, but it is not uniformly the dominant late GI complaint. Acute meta-analyses primarily involving hospitalized patients estimated diarrhea around 7-8%, whereas long-COVID studies include dyspepsia, appetite disturbance, abdominal pain, constipation, and reflux-like symptoms at comparable or higher frequencies [3,8-11]. These estimates should not be combined across disease phases. A symptom present for several weeks after an infection may still represent resolving post-infectious illness; a Rome-defined DGBI requires a chronic, pattern-based diagnosis. Prospective studies showing decreasing symptom prevalence from one to six months support this distinction [4,15]. Demographic, Geographic, and Clinical Heterogeneity The most consistent prospective risk signal is the presence of GI symptoms during acute infection, with some cohorts also identifying greater acute disease severity and psychological comorbidity as predictors of later DGBI [4,15]. Evidence for a universal effect of sex, age, vaccination status, or variant is less consistent. Large database studies can adjust for measured comorbidities but incompletely capture diet, antibiotic exposure, access to care, health-seeking behavior, and pre-infection microbiome composition [1,2]. Variant and vaccination eras also overlap with changes in hospitalization practices and treatment, making causal attribution difficult. Accordingly, demographic or geographic differences should be interpreted as context-dependent rather than as a single reproducible risk profile. Pathophysiology and Mechanistic Evidence Figure 1 summarizes a plausible mechanistic framework while emphasizing that no single causal chain has been established. Many data supporting ACE2 perturbation, cytokine activation, permeability changes, and dysbiosis derive from acute infection or broad post-acute syndromes rather than patients with chronic diarrhea meeting Rome criteria [7,18-31]. Intestinal Infection, ACE2, and Viral Persistence The intestinal epithelium expresses ACE2 and entry-associated proteases, and experimental and clinical data support intestinal involvement during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection [7,20,23,27,29]. Altered ACE2-related signaling may affect amino-acid transport, antimicrobial peptide expression, epithelial integrity, and local immune regulation. These observations provide biologic plausibility but do not establish that ACE2 disruption persists as the cause of chronic diarrhea. Viral persistence requires careful terminology. In a longitudinal study of 113 people with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, fecal SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 12.7% at four months and 3.8% at seven months, demonstrating prolonged RNA shedding but not necessarily replication-competent virus [21]. In an endoscopic study of 46 patients with inflammatory bowel disease approximately seven months after COVID-19, gut mucosal viral RNA was detected in 32 and nucleocapsid protein in 24; importantly, investigators were unable to culture virus from tissue [22]. This selected IBD cohort is not equivalent to a population with post-COVID functional diarrhea. Thus, RNA detection, antigen persistence, viable virus, and causal persistence-related diarrhea are distinct claims; only the first two have substantial human evidence in selected cohorts. Immune Activation and Mucosal Barrier Dysfunction Acute COVID-19 can produce cytokine and chemokine activation, epithelial injury, and markers compatible with increased intestinal permeability [7,18,26,27]. Barrier disruption can expose mucosal immune cells to microbial products and alter secretion or motility. However, direct evidence linking persistent cytokine activation or permeability abnormalities specifically to chronic post-COVID functional diarrhea is limited. Available post-acute studies often evaluate broad multisystem symptoms, small selected cohorts, or surrogate biomarkers rather than a well-phenotyped diarrhea endpoint. The most defensible interpretation is therefore that immune and barrier abnormalities are plausible contributors whose causal magnitude in chronic diarrhea remains uncertain. Microbiome, Microbial Taxa, and Metabolites Acute COVID-19 microbiome studies repeatedly report depletion of potentially beneficial commensals. In a two-hospital cohort, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, and bifidobacteria were underrepresented and remained reduced in serial samples collected up to 30 days after disease resolution [30]. In a prospective PACS cohort, patients with symptoms at six months had higher Ruminococcus gnavus and Bacteroides vulgatus and lower F. prausnitzii; butyrate-producing Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and F. prausnitzii showed inverse correlations with PACS [28]. These PACS symptoms were predominantly non-GI, so the findings cannot be assumed to explain chronic diarrhea. Functional microbial changes may be as important as taxonomic shifts. In 66 antibiotic-naive COVID-19 patients, pathways for short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) and L-isoleucine biosynthesis were impaired and remained abnormal beyond 30 days after recovery; measured fecal SCFAs were also lower, with associations to severity and inflammatory markers [18]. GI-specific post-acute data are more limited but emerging; a study that followed 983 antibiotic-naive patients with mild COVID-19 identified distinct oral/gut microbial and serum metabolomic patterns in a small subset with GI symptoms at three months [31]. Bile-acid and tryptophan alterations have also been reported in acute/severe COVID-19 studies, but direct evidence connecting a specific bile-acid signature to persistent post-COVID functional diarrhea remains insufficient [25]. Confounding is a major limitation. Antibiotics, hospitalization, diet, geography, medications, acute disease severity, and baseline health can independently alter microbiome composition. Antibiotic-naive designs reduce one source of confounding, but most studies do not fully control diet, pre-infection microbiota, socioeconomic context, or all medication exposures [18,31]. Chronic diarrhea itself can alter microbial composition, creating reverse causation. Microbiome findings should therefore be interpreted as associations until longitudinal, pre-infection, functionally characterized studies demonstrate directionality. Gut-Brain and Proposed Gut-Lung Interactions The gut-brain axis integrates enteric neural, central nervous system, immune, endocrine, and microbial signaling. Post-infectious inflammation, stress, sleep disruption, altered diet, and changes in activity can interact with visceral sensitivity and motility without implying that symptoms are purely psychological [5,6,32]. This framework is well aligned with DGBI biology. By contrast, gut-lung communication is biologically plausible and relevant to systemic inflammation, but its specific role in chronic post-COVID diarrhea has not been established; it should be considered a proposed or incompletely defined pathway rather than a proven mechanism [25,26]. Figure 1 summarizes the proposed mechanisms linking SARS-CoV-2 infection with persistent gastrointestinal symptoms and disorders of gut-brain interaction. Table 3 summarizes the proposed mechanisms and the strength and limitations of current human evidence. Clinical Phenotypes and Relationship to PI-IBS Post-COVID bowel dysfunction may represent several different clinical pathways as follows: slow resolution of acute infectious diarrhea, an organic or medication-related disorder unmasked during/after infection, a new DGBI triggered by infection, or exacerbation of a pre-existing bowel disorder. The overlap with PI-IBS is substantial because both can follow infection and involve altered barrier function, low-grade immune activation, dysbiosis, visceral hypersensitivity, and gut-brain signaling [5,14,15,32]. Current evidence does not establish post-COVID bowel dysfunction as a single distinct disease entity. For a patient who develops classic IBS after COVID-19 and meets Rome criteria, COVID-19 is best conceptualized as a potential infectious trigger unless future biomarkers demonstrate a reproducibly distinct pathobiology. Duration is clinically important. Loose stools lasting days to a few weeks after acute illness can reflect transient recovery or treatment effects. What is Cicada COVID... Does it come from insects? The name "Cicada" is just a nickname used for the BA.3.2 variant for easy international recognition. It is not related to insects and is not transmitted through insects in any way. Is it different or more severe than previous variants? Mutations: More than 50 genetic changes have been found, especially in the spike protein area, which helps the virus enter human cells and evade the immune system more effectively. Severity: From laboratory data, "there is no evidence yet that it causes increased severity" compared to other Omicron variants currently circulating. Its replication and transmission behavior remain at similar levels. Has it reached Thailand yet... Anything to worry about? Based on current surveillance and genomic sequencing, "no reports of the Cicada variant have been found in Thailand yet." It is mostly detected in small proportions (about 5-8%) in some countries such as South Africa, Australia, and the United States, so it is not the dominant variant globally at this time. How to prepare... Is there a vaccine yet? Currently, there is no vaccine specifically produced for the Cicada variant. However, having basic immunity still helps reduce the severity of the disease. The important thing is to take care of yourself according to familiar measures: Wash your hands frequently and avoid crowded places. Wear a mask when in high-risk areas or poorly ventilated spaces. Monitor for unusual symptoms such as fever, cough, or difficulty breathing. If symptoms occur, perform an ATK test and consult a doctor for an accurate diagnosis.
