supplementary_news.content: Business&Talent Good News Barcelona Barcelona in figures Made in Barcelona Professionals Barcelona Global Young Talent Arts Events The Barcelonian The Bar of the Post Letters Music Scene Creativity Images Lifestyle Gastronomy Baco & Boca Hotels with history The Radar Unknown Faces Enjoy Barcelona From La Rambla to the world Interviews: A Granini with... Interviews: A 'ColaCao' with... Opinion Live Focus Espectacles BCN Close the sidebar Good News Barcelona The European Medicines Agency gives green light to Hipra vaccine The Catalan family business makes history in the medical and pharmaceutical sector by managing to commercialize the first COVID vaccine developed 100% in the European Union. Although the pandemic has subsided, its factory in Amer (Girona) is prepared to manufacture up to 600 million doses per year, which it will sell under the Bimervax brand at a price between 9.75 and 7 euros. Sergi Saborit 31 march of 2023 at 09:55h It has been a long time coming, but, finally, this Thursday Hipra has obtained the positive opinion from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) essential for the European Union to authorize the start of commercialization of its vaccine against covid-19, named Bimervax. According to the Catalan family company, in "a matter of hours" the European Commission will issue this authorization, which represents a historic milestone for the Catalan scientific and pharmaceutical sector and for Spain as a whole, as it is the first vaccine developed 100% in the European Union. Bimervax is also the first bivalent adjuvanted recombinant protein vaccine authorized in the EU against this virus, which gives it a differential character compared to the vaccines mostly used until now, based on messenger RNA technology. According to Hipra, it is a vaccine for people over 16 years of age especially indicated as a booster dose and that can help increase vaccination rates, as it causes fewer reactions and offers a "superior" duration of immunity compared to the vaccines previously on the market. "We have developed a vaccine that is very safe and, furthermore, it is less reactogenic than RNA vaccines, which represents a clear advantage for the population reluctant to vaccinate, tolerance is much better," assures Elia Torrella, executive vice president of Hipra and R&D director. According to the executive, Bimervax offers a very powerful "boost" as a fourth dose, provides protection against all existing variants of the virus and, furthermore, has the advantage that its logistics are very simple because it is "ready to use" ---it does not need to be reconstituted before use--- and because it does not require freezing: it must be stored refrigerated at a temperature between 2 and 8 degrees. "For Hipra, today is a very exciting and long-awaited day," said Torrella, who emphasizes that the new vaccine is the result "of the company's knowledge" and also of its "enthusiasm, perseverance and optimism" with the project. Unlike other pharmaceutical companies, Hipra has shown total transparency regarding the price of the new vaccine: each dose will cost between 9.75 euros and 7 euros, depending on the volume of purchase made by each State. And when can the first doses of Bimervax be injected? This is a decision that depends exclusively on the health authorities of the countries and the vaccination plans they activate, but Hipra assures that, in the best case, by the end of April they could deliver the vaccine to the warehouses that supply health centers. "We have enough stock of finished product and raw material to be able to supply all the vaccines they ask for during these first months," assures Carles Fàbrega, Hipra's human health director. According to the executive, the production capacity of the Amer (Girona) plant is 600 million doses per year, although this figure could be expanded to 1,000 million if necessary. Hipra has been manufacturing the Bimervax vaccine for months, which it can now start selling. The Girona-based company has already signed a pre-contract with 13 countries of the European Union that have the right ---though not the obligation--- to purchase up to 250 million doses. Of these 13 countries, a group of six ---including Spain--- had already communicated to the company their intention to make the first purchases once community authorization was obtained, so the first contracts could be formalized in the coming weeks. In parallel, Hipra is in negotiations with other non-EU countries, such as Malaysia and some states in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia, but everything was on stand by awaiting the EMA's decision. "Now we will begin the registration phase in the rest of the countries of the world and we will also request WHO authorization," explained Fàbrega. The company of the Nogareda family, which until now had focused solely on veterinary vaccines, has not wanted to reveal the amount of the investment it has made for the development of Bimervax, but assures that it is the "greatest economic and human effort" made to date. The bulk of the investment has been financed with its own resources, although Hipra has also received two public loans from the Center for Industrial Technological Development (CDTI) totaling 14.7 million euros, of which 10.82 million must be repaid. Economic impact due to approval delay The evaluation period for the vaccine by the European Medicines Agency has been longer than expected, as authorization has taken almost 12 months to arrive, compared to the express approvals of four months achieved by the first vaccines in the most acute phase of the pandemic. Hipra admits that this delay has had a negative economic impact because "it hinders market entry," in the sense that commercialization begins at a less opportune moment, as countries have high stocks of competitor vaccines and, furthermore, there is a widespread perception that the pandemic has already passed, which has led to a drastic drop in revaccination rates. Elia Torrella and Carles Fàbrega during this Thursday's press conference. "Covid-19 is here to stay; there is a general scientific consensus that it will be necessary to continue vaccinating, especially certain population groups. It is very important to have more vaccines to keep covid under control, so there is clearly space in the market for a vaccine like Bimervax, we are very happy to have finally received approval," Torrella highlighted. Along the same lines, Fàbrega defends that the new Catalan vaccine "fits perfectly with the needs of the global population," although he declined to make sales forecasts for this first year. Hipra also highlights another factor that states should consider when deciding whether or not to acquire their vaccine: "it is not good to vaccinate exclusively with a single technology", referring to the fact that currently the vaccines supplied are RNA and not recombinant protein. According to Torrella, the system they have used "facilitates the body's immune response" by introducing into the body a protein previously designed in a laboratory that generates antibodies, instead of the cells performing this step. Furthermore, it is a bivalent vaccine, which means that instead of one, it contains two proteins to fight against two different variants, in this case Beta and Alpha of SARS-CoV-2. "It is a much more versatile vaccine, because it is a two-in-one", Torrella pointed out, after noting that if new variants appeared, the vaccine could be adapted in just four months. Bimervax technology is widely used and known in vaccine manufacturing, such as for hepatitis and influenza. Hipra carries out the entire production process in Amer, which allows it to gain response capacity. The board has thanked the entire team of Hipra professionals for the enormous effort made and, especially, all the volunteers who participated in the clinical trials that were necessary to obtain the EMA's approval. According to Hipra, the EMA's positive opinion comes after concluding that "it has sufficient solid data on the quality, immunogenicity and safety of the vaccine." "In phase IIb and III studies, it has been shown that it is a safe, low-reactogenic vaccine with a broad capacity to neutralize the main variants of SARS-CoV-2, including the Omicron variants. In the comparative study versus the mRNA vaccine required by the EMA, it is shown that, 6 months after receiving the booster dose, people vaccinated with the Hipra vaccine present higher levels of neutralizing antibodies against all the variants studied, which suggests more lasting protection. In the same comparative study, it is shown to have less reactogenicity than the RNA vaccine," they add. Filed in Good News Barcelona User Consent Prompt Focus Prompt

OffOn Stream on WHO says suspected hantavirus cluster 'is not the start of a COVID pandemic' There are 12 suspected cases so far. ByMary Kekatos and Zoe Magee May 7, 2026, 4:39 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google An epidemiologist from the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday that the suspected hantavirus cluster aboard a cruise ship is not the beginning of another COVID-19 pandemic. Eight cases are currently being reported by the WHO, including five laboratory-confirmed cases and three suspected cases. Of those eight cases, three have died. Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, an infectious disease epidemiologist and acting director of epidemic and pandemic management at the WHO, was asked during a press conference what the difference was between this cluster and the early days of the COVID pandemic. Related Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US "I want to be unequivocal here. This is not SARS-CoV-2. This is not the start of a COVID pandemic. This is an outbreak that we see on a ship," Van Kerkhove said. Van Kerkhove explained that hantavirus doesn't spread in the same way that coronaviruses do, but rather through "close, intimate contact." Most hantaviruses don't transmit from person to person. "The actions that are being taken on board [the ship] are precautionary to prevent any onward spread," she added. Health personnel assisting patients onto a boat from the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images There appears to be two confirmed cases and four suspected cases that have not been added to the WHO's official count yet. The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport confirmed that two patients infected with the virus are currently hospitalized in the Netherlands, one at Radboud University Medical Center and the other at Leiden University Medical Center. Additionally, two Singapore residents who were on board the ship are currently being monitored. Singapore's Communicable Diseases Agency said it was notified of the individuals on May 4 and 5. "They have been isolated at the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, where they are being tested for hantavirus. The risk to the general public in Singapore is currently low," the agency said. The agency added that test results are pending, with one resident having a runny nose. The other is asymptomatic. The French Health Ministry also issued a statement on Thursday that a French national has been tested after they displayed mild symptoms. This person had been in contact with one of the confirmed cases. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Three deaths have been recorded so far, including a married Dutch couple. The 70-year-old male patient died on April 11, and his body was taken off the ship on the island of St. Helena on April 24. His 69-year-old wife disembarked on the same day, and her health rapidly deteriorated. She died at a South Africa hospital on April 26. A third passenger, a German woman, presented with pneumonia symptoms starting on April 28, according to the WHO. The woman died on May 2 from causes not yet known, according to Oceanwide Expeditions, which operates the cruise ship. The WHO said 29 people disembarked on St. Helena on the same day that the body of the Dutch male patient and his wife disembarked. They traveled to 12 countries: Canada, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, Great Britain, St. Kitts and Nevis, Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Sweden, Turkey and the United States. Popular Reads Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys 2 days ago Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials 13 hours ago District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Sep 29 The disembarked guests have all been contacted by Oceanwide Expeditions. In the U.S., local authorities in five states -- Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas and Virginia -- are monitoring the disembarked passengers and are conducting contact tracing, None have shown signs of illness at this time. Anais Legend, technical lead for viral hemorrhagic fevers at WHO, said during the press conference on Thursday that "step-by-step guidance is being developed" for the disembarked passengers and that the WHO is coordinating with national authorities. Anyone with any signs of symptoms will be isolated while other passengers have their risk exposure evaluated. The cruise ship MV Hondius, carrying passengers suspected of having cases of hantavirus on board, leaves Praia, Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. Reuters Public health experts said they expected a more robust response from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health. "CDC would typically be asked by WHO to, or by a country to, help in technical assistance," Dr. Carlos del Rio, an H. Cliff Sauls distinguished professor of medicine at the Emory University School of Medicine, told reporters on Thursday. Typically, CDC teams would be deployed to an area, he said, and the teams would perform contact tracing and interviews and conduct an outbreak investigation. "I would envision by now, many, many days ago, we would have seen ... a team from CDC deployed to the area," he added. Related 3 dead in suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship: What to know Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the IDSA, added that she would have expected a CDC press briefing, an alert from the agency's Health Alert Network or information from the NIH on potential treatments in the pipeline that could receive emergency use authorization to help treat hantavirus patients. Marrazzo said she is not aware that conversations about potential therapies at NIH aren't happening but it "does not give me a lot of assurance or reassurance that we're not hearing about any of it." The CDC posted a statement on X on Wednesday on behalf of NIH Director and acting CDC director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that read, "Our hearts go out to the passengers aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius and their families during this difficult time. Our CDC team began coordinating with domestic and international partners as soon as we were notified of a hantavirus situation." The statement said there is "clear, written health guidance to the American passengers through the State Department" and that the CDC "will continue to update as more information becomes available and remains committed to protecting the health and safety of the American public." The agency also published a statement on its website stating that the Trump administration "is closely monitoring the situation" and that the Department of State "is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." The CDC also said the risk to the American public is "extremely low." The WHO said during Thursday's press briefing that the U.S. is coordinating with the global health agency in a technical capacity. Because the cluster is limited and confined to a cruise ship, the "idea of sending messages across the world and panicking everyone is not required," said Dr. Abdirahman Mahmoud, director of the WHO's health emergency alert and response operations. He added that the WHO is "informally" aware that contact tracing has been done of the U.S. passengers who disembarked last month and are back home. supplementary_news.content_title: New ‘atlas’ of respiratory infections suggests Covid is no longer just a winter virus
supplementary_news.content: Oriol Güell Barcelona - OCT 02, 2026 - 04:40 EDT Share on Whatsapp Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prefer EL PAÍS on Google Compartir: Whatsapp Facebook Twitter Bluesky Linkedin Copy link A comprehensive atlas of the 18 main respiratory viruses circulating in Catalonia, produced for the first time in Spain by researchers from that northeastern region, reveals that the coronavirus that caused the Covid-16 pandemic — SARS-CoV-2 — “is currently not a winter virus. In recent years, it has shown clear peaks during the spring and summer, which is different from what was initially expected.” This behavior has caused a clear mismatch with the current vaccination calendar . “We are immunizing at-risk groups [older people, those with chronic illnesses...] in the autumn, when the virus’ epidemic waves have already passed, and not beforehand, as would be desirable. This work raises the possibility that it may be necessary to adjust the planning of vaccination campaigns and guidelines,” warns Jacobo Mendioroz, deputy director general for Surveillance and Public Health of the Catalan government. The research’s findings, based on Catalonia’s healthcare system data between 2022 and 2025, have been observed this year again in the real world. Coronavirus incidence surged at the end of summer, when communities had not yet begun the vaccination campaign against this pathogen, which is administered alongside the flu shot. The new research highlights SARS-CoV-2’s behavior, more erratic after the pandemic but now showing mainly “a clear summer epidemic pattern .” Juan Carlos Galán, head of Virology at Ramón y Cajal Hospital in Madrid, considers the research highly relevant but says it is still too early to classify the coronavirus as exclusively a summer virus: “There are recent data from other European countries, and some areas of Spain, that point more to a biennial incidence, in summer and winter. What was observed in Catalonia over these three seasons indicates a trend in SARS-CoV-2 behavior, but we do not know whether other viral or environmental factors could have impacted that finding and we will have to wait for the next seasons to confirm it.” This expert highlights the study’s contribution to a “fascinating field” he calls viral ecology. “We see that there are interferences and, at times, what appears to be competition among different viruses. A good example was the first year of the pandemic, when influenza disappeared completely, overwhelmed by covid. This apparent antagonism between flu and SARS-CoV-2 is observed in subsequent years. Each virus unfolds on the calendar in an orderly way, as if occupying different niches. Many factors intervene in this process, even if they are not fully understood,” he concludes. Changing vaccination campaigns For Gregorio Montes Salas, secretary general of the Spanish Society of Preventive Medicine, Public Health and Healthcare Management (SEMPSPGS), the study confirms that “the coronavirus has not followed the expected winter pattern, at least so far.” He adds that this raises the option of “considering the possibility of de-seasonalizing vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.” Mendioroz and Montes Salas agree that before making decisions “it will be necessary to wait for further research,” given the logistical complexity of changing campaigns and the risk of undermining achieved coverage (65% for flu among those 65 and older and 50% for coronavirus). The underlying idea is that, even if belated, it is preferable for at-risk people to be immunized by taking advantage of the momentum of regional autumn campaigns rather than spreading doses across the year and losing adherence. “Campaigns make mass vaccination easier. Changing dates requires a logistical effort that must be carefully studied, but it may be something worth exploring,” Montes Salas says. “The whole organization, the messaging and even public perception would change. The risk is that coverage could drop: who is going to get vaccinated at the start of summer against a virus that has always been associated with cold weather?” adds Mendioroz. The paper was published in the latest issue of Eurosurveillance — the scientific journal of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) — and its main aim was to obtain a detailed picture of respiratory virus circulation. “Influenza has always been monitored and, more recently, Covid and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). But what about the others? The answer provides key information: it helps plan prevention measures, prepare health centers or hospitals for peaks in demand and even anticipate what might happen,” Mendioroz says. One reason this is possible, the study’s conclusions argue, is that “respiratory viruses mainly follow a predictable pattern, appearing one after another in a consistent order every year.” “We know, for example, that the flu wave is successively preceded by a rhinovirus wave and then a parainfluenza wave,” the Generalitat’s deputy director general for Surveillance illustrates. The researchers analyzed more than 33,000 samples obtained between October 2022 and September 2025 by the Information System for Infection Surveillance in Catalonia (SIVIC), the sentinel network that monitors respiratory viruses in real time. The panel tracks the following viruses and subtypes: three influenza A strains and one B, two RSV strains, SARS-CoV-2, two seasonal coronaviruses (NL63 and OC43), four parainfluenza types, and one each of the following groups: rhinovirus, enterovirus, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and bocavirus. Influenza A shows the clearest seasonal pattern, according to the paper. Its peak usually occurs in Spain between late December and early February, although most often it happens in the second half of January. “Meanwhile, influenza B displays a less regular seasonality” and is usually offset from that peak, the researchers conclude. RSV also has a clear winter pattern, although in this case it precedes the flu by a few weeks and typically “reaches its peak roughly a month before it.” Rhinoviruses and enteroviruses, which cause mild cold-like illnesses, instead show a two-wave pattern, with peaks in autumn (September–October) and spring. Rhinovirus circulation also “declines when SARS-CoV-2 is circulating strongly,” the paper notes. Another group of pathogens that infect the respiratory tract maintains a very different profile and shows a constant presence “throughout the year, without clearly defined epidemic peaks.” This is the case for adenoviruses, some coronaviruses other than SARS-CoV-2 (such as NL63) and two parainfluenza types (1 and 4). The study also details the sequence of the remaining pathogens: parainfluenza virus 2 slightly precedes influenza, while metapneumovirus — a pathogen very common in childhood — and parainfluenza 3 emerge just as influenza begins to decline. Meanwhile, bocavirus and the seasonal coronavirus OC43 begin activity in mid-autumn, but their incidence rises slowly to reach peaks between February and April. Uthmeier alleges Pfizer misled Florida about its COVID vaccine’s safety

by Michael Moline, Florida Phoenix
October 1, 2026

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit Thursday against Pfizer Inc., alleging unfair and deceptive marketing of Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine.

The suit, filed in state trial court in St. Lucie County, also names Albert Bourla, the company’s chairman and CEO.

It seeks monetary damages for each violation of Florida law plus an injunction against future violations.

“Pfizer’s conduct misled Florida consumers when they were making some of the most sensitive health decisions of their lives. Ultimately, Pfizer’s misconduct rests on the paternalistic assumption that Florida consumers could not be trusted with the truth about Pfizer’s products. That offensive assumption is anathema to the principles underlying the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (‘FDUTPA’),” it asserts.

Uthmeier denounced the company in a video posted on X.

In response, Pfizer issued a written statement.

“We are proud to have developed the COVID-19 vaccine in record time in the midst of a global pandemic and saved countless lives. The representations made by Pfizer about its COVID-19 vaccine have been accurate and science-based, and the Company stands behind the safety and efficacy of its vaccine. Pfizer believes that the state’s allegations have no merit and will respond to the suit in due course.”

“Pfizer is deeply committed to the well-being of the patients it serves. Since its initial authorization by FDA in December 2020, the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine has been administered to billions of people, demonstrated a favorable safety profile in all age groups, and helped protect against severe COVID-19 outcomes, including hospitalization and death.”

Florida’s complaint recalls the scary time when Americans confronted a new virus that filled hospitals and impelled government leaders to close nonessential businesses, including in Florida initially.

Gov. Ron DeSantis later changed course, easing business restrictions and surrounding himself with COVID skeptics including Joseph Ladapo, whom the governor installed as Florida surgeon general.

“Florida citizens faced an unprecedented level of uncertainty” and “worried about how to protect their loved ones and themselves from a previously unknown virus” and resulting “once-in-a-generation economic shock,” the complaint reads. The company “bet big” its mRNA vaccine, it adds.

To overcome skepticism over the novel vaccine, the company undertook an intensive marketing campaign attesting to the vaccine’s safety, the document continues.

“Pfizer was not content merely to promote its own narrative. It also sought to quash any dissent that might impact consumer demand — like calling those who dared to question Pfizer’s public claims ‘criminals.’”

At the same time, the complaint says, Pfizer’s “record-breaking profits rested on deception and falsehoods. While Pfizer was insisting to consumers that the vaccine posed no material safety risks — and while it actively sought to discredit those who said otherwise — Pfizer was aware of data reflecting serious safety risks that it hid from the public.”

In January 2025, a Florida statewide grand jury found no evidence that COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers broke federal or state laws when making and distributing the shots. That was more than two years after DeSantis asked the Florida Supreme Court to assemble it to investigate alleged wrongdoing related to the COVID-19 vaccines.

The report did criticize what it considered too-close relationships between regulatory agencies such as the Food and Drug Administration and Pfizer and Moderna.

supplementary_news.content: tyla homepage tyla homepage News Politics Entertainment Celebrity Entertainment Celebrity Life Animals Food & Drink Women's Health Mental Health Sex & Relationships Travel Real Life TV & Film True Crime Tyla Recommends Astrology Beauty Hair Make-up Skincare Style Home Categories Home>Life Published 14:42 30 Sep 2026 GMT+1 Difference between Covid and flu symptoms as cases surge across UK The UKHSA has issued fresh data on the seasonal rise of Covid-19 and the flu Madison Burgess Follow us on Google Discover The September sickness has officially arrived - and people are being taken down left, right, and centre by sniffling noses, endless coughing, headaches, and high temperatures. If you’ve been forced to call in sick to work in the past few weeks, you wouldn’t be the only one, as the latest UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) data has highlighted a surge in both the flu and Covid-19 this month. As reported by The Mirror, in the week of 24 September, hospital admissions with Covid increased from 0.81 per 100,000 people to 1.2 per 100,000 people, which is an almost 50 per cent rise. However, the UKHSA has reassured that this is actually an expected level for this time of year. Advert Meanwhile, Influenza cases also increased, and the illness is currently circulating at baseline levels. Advert Emergency department attendances for influenza-like-illnessincreased also last week and were above seasonally expected levels. Seasonal illnesses are ramping up again in the UK (Getty Stock Image) As outlined by Manchester Evening News, out of those tested via a GP swab, 10.7% tested positive for flu, which is up from 8.3% the previous week. With both of these seasonal illnesses on the rise, it can be difficult to tell which one you’re actually dealing with, especially since some of the symptoms overlap. Advert The biggest difference is that a sudden loss of taste or smell is common for Covid-19, but very rare with the flu. And as per Mayo Clinic, seasonal flu symptoms usually show up quickly, about one to four days after you're around someone who is sick. Covid-19 symptoms, on the other hand, generally appear two to 14 days later. However, there are also a lot of similarities, such as fever, a dry cough, shortness of breath or trouble breathing, feeling tired, a sore throat, a headache, a runny or stuffy nose, and muscle aches. The flu and Covid-19 have a lot of similar symptoms (Getty Stock Image) Symptoms of Covid-19 As per the NHS, the most common symptoms of Covid-19 are: A high temperature – you may feel hot, cold or shivery, or your skin is hot to touch on your chest or back (you do not need to measure your temperature) A new, continuous cough – this means coughing a lot for more than an hour, or 3 or more coughing episodes in 24 hours A loss or change to your sense of smell or taste Shortness of breath Feeling tired or exhausted An aching body A headache A sore throat A blocked or runny nose Loss of appetite Diarrhoea Feeling sick or being sick The NHS advises that if you think you have Covid-19, you should try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people if you or your child have symptoms and either: Have a high temperature Do not feel well enough to go to work, school, childcare, or do your normal activities You can go back to your normal activities when you feel better or do not have a high temperature, and if your child has mild symptoms such as a runny nose, sore throat, or mild cough, and they feel well enough, they can go to school or childcare. Advert Last week, hospital admissions with Covid increased from 0.81 per 100,000 people to 1.2 per 100,000 people (Getty Stock Image) Symptoms of flu Flu symptoms come on very quickly and can include: A sudden high temperature An aching body Feeling tired or exhausted A dry cough A sore throat A headache Difficulty sleeping Loss of appetite The symptoms are similar for children, but they can also have ear pain, sore eyes, swollen glands, and appear less active. Advert You can find more information about both Covid-19 and the flu on the NHS website.
